# Trace an AI agent with Neatlogs

Set up Neatlogs tracing in this working directory. Follow these steps in order.

## Step 1: Set up Neatlogs access

Neatlogs project ID: `110108af-1737-47ee-8494-cf482d13defd`

Set `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` to the key below in the shell the user will run the app from,
for example `export NEATLOGS_API_KEY="REDACTED"`. If the app loads a
`.env` file, add it there instead. Do not commit the key to version control.

```
REDACTED
```

Never replace this key with a guessed or invented one. This is an SDK project key, not a public API CLI credential. SDK Doctor verification can use it without CLI login. CLI readback requires browser/device approval or a service-account token; if neither is available, mark that step "waiting on a human" and continue SDK verification.

The CLI host is the dashboard origin `https://app.neatlogs.com`, not the ingest endpoint. Use this host explicitly on every CLI command.

## Step 2: Detect the language and stack

Look at the workspace and determine the language and which LLM providers / agent frameworks it uses. If the project spans more than one language, instrument each one. If the project is a monorepo, check the git root to get oriented, but only ever instrument services in or below the current working directory — never a sibling or parent app outside it, even if a workspace/compose config references one.

**Finding independent services.** A monorepo can bundle several independently-deployable services; each one that reaches an LLM/agent/tool call gets treated as its own entry point later (own workflow name in Step 4) — skip health/readiness/CRUD-only services that never call a model entirely. Check these signals in order and stop at the first one that finds more than one service directory:

1. **Workspace config** (most authoritative) — a `workspaces` field in the root `package.json`, or a `packages` field in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. Resolve those glob patterns to directories, then keep only the ones that actually have their own manifest (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, etc.) — a glob can match a plain non-package directory too.
2. **docker-compose** — `docker-compose.yml`/`docker-compose.yaml`/`compose.yml`/`compose.yaml` at the root. Each entry under `services:` whose `build` (a plain string, or an object's `context` field) resolves to an existing directory is one service.
3. **Scattered manifests** (fallback, only if neither signal above found more than one) — search for manifest files (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, etc.) up to 4 directories deep, excluding `node_modules`, `.git`, `dist`, `build`, `.next`, `venv`, `.venv`, **`pycache`**, `target`, `.turbo`, `vendor`. Drop the repo root's own manifest (that's the whole-repo language, not a separate service) and drop any candidate directory that's nested inside another candidate — a service's own internal shared-lib subpackage is not a separate service.

Edge case: if exactly one of these signals finds exactly one nested service, and the repo root itself has no manifest/language of its own, use that single nested directory as the actual service root instead of the top-level directory — it IS the real service, just not living at the repo root (e.g. a `services/api/` with nothing else at the top level).

If none of the three signals finds more than one candidate, treat the whole repo at the current working directory as a single service — this is the common case, and nothing else here changes for it. For every service found this way, only keep it if it reaches an LLM/agent/tool call — drop the rest, per the CRUD/health-check exclusion above.

**Identifying entry points within each service.** A single service usually has several independent, separately-triggerable capabilities — these are the actual entry points, not the service as a whole. Typical shapes: an HTTP route, a CLI command/subcommand, a cron/scheduled job, a queue/stream consumer (Kafka/SQS/Celery/RabbitMQ/BullMQ — one entry point per message/task type, not one for the whole consumer loop), a webhook/event handler, an agent-loop iteration, or a public library API function. Two things commonly get this wrong:

- **Altitude** — an internal helper the entry point calls into (`run_pipeline`, `process_document`, `process_chunk`) is NOT itself an entry point; the entry point is the outer route/command/job that calls it.
- **Multiplexed entry** — if one transport dispatches to several different capabilities (a single `/run` route branching on a `task_type` field, a Celery task branching by job kind, an argparse dispatcher, a Kafka consumer loop branching on `msg.topic`/`event_type`), treat EACH BRANCH as its own entry point — never the shared dispatcher as one entry point covering all of them.

For each entry point, also note its process kind — it changes how you initialize and where spans root:

- **One-shot script**: initialize once near the top, and end by flushing/shutting down the SDK (its process exits immediately after, and unflushed spans batched in memory are otherwise lost).
- **Long-running server**: initialize once at process startup — never inside a request handler — and only flush/shut down on process shutdown, not per request. Root each request under its own span (e.g. a `WORKFLOW` on the handler) so concurrent requests don't share one trace.
- **Concurrent operations within one entry point** (goroutines, worker threads, manual thread pools — not plain `async`/`await` in the same coroutine, which propagates context on its own): context does not always propagate automatically across a new thread or goroutine. Check Step 3's reference for whether this language/runtime requires threading the trace context through explicitly (Go always does) or handles it for you.

Neatlogs has a native SDK for Python, TypeScript, and Go — if the detected language is one of those, continue to Step 3. For any OTHER language, there is no Neatlogs SDK; pick ONE of these two paths instead, and skip Step 3 (its SDK integration-mechanism guidance is not applicable here):

- **Default: the dependency-free HTTP endpoint.** Use this unless the app already has OpenTelemetry, or the language's OTel support is clearly the more idiomatic fit (e.g. Java, .NET). Follow https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/http-injection exactly, but send to the regional URL `https://ingest.neatlogs.com/v1/trace` instead of any default host shown in the guide. The mechanism is fundamentally different from Steps 3–4 below: build ONE nested JSON tree (an object with a `children` array) as the code for one entry-point invocation runs, then send it as a SINGLE `POST /v1/trace` when that invocation completes — success or error, so wrap the send in this language's try/finally-equivalent. Never POST once per span; that violates the endpoint's contract and produces disconnected traces instead of one.
- **OpenTelemetry / OTLP-gRPC, when the app already emits OpenTelemetry spans** (its own `tracer.start_span()`-style setup, an OTel Collector, or a GenAI-instrumented framework) **or you're setting one up now:** if there's no existing OTel SDK for this language yet, find and install the official one from https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/ (its own site — Neatlogs doesn't ship or document per-language OTel setup beyond Python/TS/Go) and add a standard gRPC trace exporter. Either way, point the exporter at Neatlogs: endpoint `ingest.neatlogs.com:443`, gRPC protocol, and the project key sent as the `x-api-key` gRPC metadata key — NOT an `Authorization: Bearer` header. Standard: emit spans following the official OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) — `gen_ai.system`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.operation.name`, token/usage attributes, etc. (If this happens to be a TypeScript app already using the Vercel AI SDK's own built-in `experimental_telemetry` rather than the Neatlogs SDK, its native `ai.*` attribute format — `ai.prompt`, `ai.response.text`, `ai.operationId`, etc. — is also recognized directly; no need to convert it to `gen_ai.*`.) Spans that don't follow either of these two shapes still get ingested, but arrive as generic, unparsed spans — no model name, no token counts, no LLM-specific rendering in the dashboard. Full transport detail (including the "flush before the process exits or batched spans are silently dropped" footgun): https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/opentelemetry.

## Step 3: Follow the SDK's instrumentation reference

Python, TypeScript, or Go only — skip this step if you took one of the two paths above instead.

For each language, read the matching page and follow it exactly for HOW to capture LLM/framework calls — it lists, per provider and per framework, whether that one needs `wrap()`, `instrumentations=[...]`, or a dedicated integration helper, and that list changes as the SDK evolves, so don't guess or reuse a pattern from a different provider.

| Language | Guide |
| --- | ------|
| Python | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/python |
| TypeScript | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript |
| Go | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/go |

Use the regional Neatlogs ingest endpoint `https://ingest.neatlogs.com` for SDK initialization. Follow the language guide for the exact endpoint parameter.

## Step 4: Install and initialize the SDK

Python, TypeScript, or Go only — if you took the OpenTelemetry or HTTP-injection path in Step 2, follow that page's own setup instructions instead of this step.

- Install the SDK using this language's own package manager (`pip`/`poetry` for Python, `npm`/`pnpm`/`yarn` for TypeScript, `go get` for Go — see Step 3's reference for the exact package/module name). Look up and install the latest version rather than pinning to a specific one. Verify the install succeeded.
- Initialize the SDK once, near the app's entry point — the exact call signature (parameter names, casing, whether the API key is passed explicitly or read from the environment automatically) differs by language, so use Step 3's reference for the precise syntax rather than guessing from another language's example. Whatever the signature, never hardcode the API key. Set the workflow name to describe the specific task or pipeline this process runs — e.g. `invoice-ocr`, `support-agent`, `checkout-flow` — not the repo or app name; the project (selected by the API key) already identifies the app. If the repo has multiple independent entry points that each reach an LLM/agent/tool, give each its own workflow name describing what THAT one does.
- Calling `init()` again with the same configuration is idempotent; calling it with conflicting configuration raises a configuration error until the current SDK generation is shut down. Never add a second `init()` to switch projects inside one running process. Almost every independent entry point you find stays on the same project and is distinguished by its own workflow root. Use a secondary client only when telemetry genuinely belongs to a different Neatlogs project (for example, explicit multi-tenant routing), and confirm that ownership decision with the user rather than inferring it from code structure.
- Capture each LLM/framework call using the mechanism Step 3's reference says to use for that specific provider or framework — do not wrap something the guide says to instrument a different way, and never apply two mechanisms to the same call (e.g. `wrap()` a client AND also list it in `instrumentations=[...]`).
- `wrap()`/`instrumentations=[...]`/framework integrations only capture library calls. Add a manual `@neatlogs.span(kind="WORKFLOW")` / `trace()` around a feature entry point only when you need to GROUP several of those calls under one named trace — not as an alternative way to capture a single call.

## Step 5: Verify instrumentation and ingestion

Use the language guide to run the installed SDK's `doctor --local` and `doctor --probe` commands with the SDK project key and regional ingest endpoint. These are SDK commands, not subcommands of `neatlogs-cli`. Do not guess the Python, TypeScript, or Go invocation. For HTTP/OTLP-only integrations, follow their guide's verification path instead.

Do not run the application yourself. Ask the user to run an instrumented entry point and provide its trace ID or result. A synthetic Doctor probe verifies the telemetry pipeline; report it separately from verification of the user's actual application trace. Do not claim application instrumentation passed based only on a synthetic probe. With only the SDK project key, use Doctor readback and mark CLI readback "waiting on a human".

## Step 6: Optional public API CLI readback

Install `neatlogs-cli` using `npm install --global neatlogs-cli` and check `neatlogs --version` (Node.js 22 or 24). The SDK key must remain available to the application, but it must not override CLI authentication.

Use the dashboard-specific profile `setup-https---app-neatlogs-com` consistently for login and every read. Before signing in, inspect `neatlogs --host https://app.neatlogs.com profile list`. Reuse this name only if it is unused or already belongs to this exact dashboard origin; otherwise choose an unused name and replace it in every command below. Login creates the profile when needed. Do not rebind an authenticated profile from another dashboard or rely on the default/active profile.

For human OAuth, the following POSIX-shell commands exclude SDK/environment credentials only from each CLI process; they do not unset the application's key. In other shells, launch the CLI in an environment without those variables. A CLI version exposing `--credential-source profile` in `--help` can use that option instead of excluding the two credential variables.

```bash
env -u NEATLOGS_API_KEY -u NEATLOGS_TOKEN neatlogs --host https://app.neatlogs.com --profile setup-https---app-neatlogs-com auth login --device
# The user must approve the displayed code in their browser.
env -u NEATLOGS_API_KEY -u NEATLOGS_TOKEN -u NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID neatlogs --host https://app.neatlogs.com --profile setup-https---app-neatlogs-com projects list
env -u NEATLOGS_API_KEY -u NEATLOGS_TOKEN neatlogs --host https://app.neatlogs.com --profile setup-https---app-neatlogs-com --project 110108af-1737-47ee-8494-cf482d13defd whoami
env -u NEATLOGS_API_KEY -u NEATLOGS_TOKEN neatlogs --host https://app.neatlogs.com --profile setup-https---app-neatlogs-com --project 110108af-1737-47ee-8494-cf482d13defd traces list --limit 10
env -u NEATLOGS_API_KEY -u NEATLOGS_TOKEN neatlogs --host https://app.neatlogs.com --profile setup-https---app-neatlogs-com --project 110108af-1737-47ee-8494-cf482d13defd traces get <trace-id>
```

Confirm the project UUID against `projects list`; discovery must not receive `--project` or `NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID`. A service-account token supplied securely via `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` can replace interactive login: exclude only `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` for those invocations, or use `--credential-source token` when supported. It needs `context:read` for discovery/whoami and `observability:read` for trace reads, plus access to the selected project. Never ask the user to paste tokens into chat.

Use the project-scoped `whoami` and actual trace read as the authoritative check. Older CLI versions can report `auth status` as authenticated just because a key is present. The command is `traces get`, not `trace get`. Trace detail returns status, token totals and span counts; use `traces spans list <trace-id>` with the same host/profile/project/credential setup for individual spans. A nonexistent trace should return `NOT_FOUND`.

## Rules

- Add only tracing. Do not set up detections, alerts, evals, or anything else.
- Make only the code changes needed to add tracing. Do not run the application yourself, and do not break or meaningfully modify existing code.
- Do not use the Neatlogs wizard CLI (`npx @neatlogs/wizard@latest`) — that's a separate, more thorough path; this prompt is the manual alternative for when it isn't available.

Full documentation index: https://docs.neatlogs.com/llms.txt

If any framework detected in Step 2 has a dedicated skill at https://github.com/neatlogs/skills (check that repo's `skill-menu.json` for the matching package, e.g. a CrewAI or LangChain project), fetch and read it before instrumenting that framework — it carries gotcha-level detail Step 3's reference doesn't (e.g. exact span-double-firing traps, per-framework attachment rules) and is worth the extra step for that framework's correctness.
```". Read the answers carefully — they may request clarification, changes, or that you not proceed — and follow what they actually say.

For every service found this way, only keep it if it reaches an LLM/agent/tool call — drop the rest, per the CRUD/health-check exclusion above.

**Identifying entry points within each service.** A single service usually has several independent, separately-triggerable capabilities — these are the actual entry points, not the service as a whole. Typical shapes: an HTTP route, a CLI command/subcommand, a cron/scheduled job, a queue/stream consumer (Kafka/SQS/Celery/RabbitMQ/BullMQ — one entry point per message/task type, not one for the whole consumer loop), a webhook/event handler, an agent-loop iteration, or a public library API function. Two things commonly get this wrong:

- **Altitude** — an internal helper the entry point calls into (`run_pipeline`, `process_document`, `process_chunk`) is NOT itself an entry point; the entry point is the outer route/command/job that calls it.
- **Multiplexed entry** — if one transport dispatches to several different capabilities (a single `/run` route branching on a `task_type` field, a Celery task branching by job kind, an argparse dispatcher, a Kafka consumer loop branching on `msg.topic`/`event_type`), treat EACH BRANCH as its own entry point — never the shared dispatcher as one entry point covering all of them.

For each entry point, also note its process kind — it changes how you initialize and where spans root:

- **One-shot script**: initialize once near the top, and end by flushing/shutting down the SDK (its process exits immediately after, and unflushed spans batched in memory are otherwise lost).
- **Long-running server**: initialize once at process startup — never inside a request handler — and only flush/shut down on process shutdown, not per request. Root each request under its own span (e.g. a `WORKFLOW` on the handler) so concurrent requests don't share one trace.
- **Concurrent operations within one entry point** (goroutines, worker threads, manual thread pools — not plain `async`/`await` in the same coroutine, which propagates context on its own): context does not always propagate automatically across a new thread or goroutine. Check Step 3's reference for whether this language/runtime requires threading the trace context through explicitly (Go always does) or handles it for you.

Neatlogs has a native SDK for Python, TypeScript, and Go — if the detected language is one of those, continue to Step 3. For any OTHER language, there is no Neatlogs SDK; pick ONE of these two paths instead, and skip Step 3 (its SDK integration-mechanism guidance is not applicable here):

- **Default: the dependency-free HTTP endpoint.** Use this unless the app already has OpenTelemetry, or the language's OTel support is clearly the more idiomatic fit (e.g. Java, .NET). Follow https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/http-injection exactly, but send to the regional URL `https://ingest.neatlogs.com/v1/trace` instead of any default host shown in the guide. The mechanism is fundamentally different from Steps 3–4 below: build ONE nested JSON tree (an object with a `children` array) as the code for one entry-point invocation runs, then send it as a SINGLE `POST /v1/trace` when that invocation completes — success or error, so wrap the send in this language's try/finally-equivalent. Never POST once per span; that violates the endpoint's contract and produces disconnected traces instead of one.
- **OpenTelemetry / OTLP-gRPC, when the app already emits OpenTelemetry spans** (its own `tracer.start_span()`-style setup, an OTel Collector, or a GenAI-instrumented framework) **or you're setting one up now:** if there's no existing OTel SDK for this language yet, find and install the official one from https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/ (its own site — Neatlogs doesn't ship or document per-language OTel setup beyond Python/TS/Go) and add a standard gRPC trace exporter. Either way, point the exporter at Neatlogs: endpoint `ingest.neatlogs.com:443`, gRPC protocol, and the project key sent as the `x-api-key` gRPC metadata key — NOT an `Authorization: Bearer` header. Standard: emit spans following the official OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) — `gen_ai.system`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.operation.name`, token/usage attributes, etc. (If this happens to be a TypeScript app already using the Vercel AI SDK's own built-in `experimental_telemetry` rather than the Neatlogs SDK, its native `ai.*` attribute format — `ai.prompt`, `ai.response.text`, `ai.operationId`, etc. — is also recognized directly; no need to convert it to `gen_ai.*`.) Spans that don't follow either of these two shapes still get ingested, but arrive as generic, unparsed spans — no model name, no token counts, no LLM-specific rendering in the dashboard. Full transport detail (including the "flush before the process exits or batched spans are silently dropped" footgun): https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/opentelemetry.

## Step 3: Follow the SDK's instrumentation reference

Python, TypeScript, or Go only — skip this step if you took one of the two paths above instead.

For each language, read the matching page and follow it exactly for HOW to capture LLM/framework calls — it lists, per provider and per framework, whether that one needs `wrap()`, `instrumentations=[...]`, or a dedicated integration helper, and that list changes as the SDK evolves, so don't guess or reuse a pattern from a different provider.

| Language | Guide |
| --- | ------|
| Python | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/python |
| TypeScript | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript |
| Go | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/go |

Use the regional Neatlogs ingest endpoint `https://ingest.neatlogs.com` for SDK initialization. Follow the language guide for the exact endpoint parameter.

## Step 4: Install and initialize the SDK

Python, TypeScript, or Go only — if you took the OpenTelemetry or HTTP-injection path in Step 2, follow that page's own setup instructions instead of this step.

- Install the SDK using this language's own package manager (`pip`/`poetry` for Python, `npm`/`pnpm`/`yarn` for TypeScript, `go get` for Go — see Step 3's reference for the exact package/module name). Look up and install the latest version rather than pinning to a specific one. Verify the install succeeded.
- Initialize the SDK once, near the app's entry point — the exact call signature (parameter names, casing, whether the API key is passed explicitly or read from the environment automatically) differs by language, so use Step 3's reference for the precise syntax rather than guessing from another language's example. Whatever the signature, never hardcode the API key. Set the workflow name to describe the specific task or pipeline this process runs — e.g. `invoice-ocr`, `support-agent`, `checkout-flow` — not the repo or app name; the project (selected by the API key) already identifies the app. If the repo has multiple independent entry points that each reach an LLM/agent/tool, give each its own workflow name describing what THAT one does.
- Calling `init()` again with the same configuration is idempotent; calling it with conflicting configuration raises a configuration error until the current SDK generation is shut down. Never add a second `init()` to switch projects inside one running process. Almost every independent entry point you find stays on the same project and is distinguished by its own workflow root. Use a secondary client only when telemetry genuinely belongs to a different Neatlogs project (for example, explicit multi-tenant routing), and confirm that ownership decision with the user rather than inferring it from code structure.
- Capture each LLM/framework call using the mechanism Step 3's reference says to use for that specific provider or framework — do not wrap something the guide says to instrument a different way, and never apply two mechanisms to the same call (e.g. `wrap()` a client AND also list it in `instrumentations=[...]`).
- `wrap()`/`instrumentations=[...]`/framework integrations only capture library calls. Add a manual `@neatlogs.span(kind="WORKFLOW")` / `trace()` around a feature entry point only when you need to GROUP several of those calls under one named trace — not as an alternative way to capture a single call.

## Step 5: Verify instrumentation and ingestion

Use the language guide to run the installed SDK's `doctor --local` and `doctor --probe` commands with the SDK project key and regional ingest endpoint. These are SDK commands, not subcommands of `neatlogs-cli`. Do not guess the Python, TypeScript, or Go invocation. For HTTP/OTLP-only integrations, follow their guide's verification path instead.

Do not run the application yourself. Ask the user to run an instrumented entry point and provide its trace ID or result. A synthetic Doctor probe verifies the telemetry pipeline; report it separately from verification of the user's actual application trace. Do not claim application instrumentation passed based only on a synthetic probe. With only the SDK project key, use Doctor readback and mark CLI readback "waiting on a human".

## Step 6: Optional public API CLI readback

Install `neatlogs-cli` using `npm install --global neatlogs-cli` and check `neatlogs --version` (Node.js 22 or 24). The SDK key must remain available to the application, but it must not override CLI authentication.

Use the dashboard-specific profile `setup-https---app-neatlogs-com` consistently for login and every read. Before signing in, inspect `neatlogs --host https://app.neatlogs.com profile list`. Reuse this name only if it is unused or already belongs to this exact dashboard origin; otherwise choose an unused name and replace it in every command below. Login creates the profile when needed. Do not rebind an authenticated profile from another dashboard or rely on the default/active profile.

For human OAuth, the following POSIX-shell commands exclude SDK/environment credentials only from each CLI process; they do not unset the application's key. In other shells, launch the CLI in an environment without those variables. A CLI version exposing `--credential-source profile` in `--help` can use that option instead of excluding the two credential variables.

```bash

# The user must approve the displayed code in their browser.
env -u NEATLOGS_API_KEY -u NEATLOGS_TOKEN -u NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID neatlogs --host https://app.neatlogs.com --profile setup-https---app-neatlogs-com projects list
env -u NEATLOGS_API_KEY -u NEATLOGS_TOKEN neatlogs --host https://app.neatlogs.com --profile setup-https---app-neatlogs-com --project 110108af-1737-47ee-8494-cf482d13defd whoami

Confirm the project UUID against `projects list`; discovery must not receive `--project` or `NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID`. A service-account token supplied securely via `NEATLOGS_TOKEN` can replace interactive login: exclude only `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` for those invocations, or use `--credential-source token` when supported. It needs `context:read` for discovery/whoami and `observability:read` for trace reads, plus access to the selected project. Never ask the user to paste tokens into chat.

Use the project-scoped `whoami` and actual trace read as the authoritative check. Older CLI versions can report `auth status` as authenticated just because a key is present. The command is `traces get`, not `trace get`. Trace detail returns status, token totals and span counts; use `traces spans list <trace-id>` with the same host/profile/project/credential setup for individual spans. A nonexistent trace should return `NOT_FOUND`.

## Rules

- Add only tracing. Do not set up detections, alerts, evals, or anything else.
- Make only the code changes needed to add tracing. Do not run the application yourself, and do not break or meaningfully modify existing code.
- Do not use the Neatlogs wizard CLI (`npx @neatlogs/wizard@latest`) — that's a separate, more thorough path; this prompt is the manual alternative for when it isn't available.

content.text:
Yes, it can run on your Pro plan, but there are limits.

**How T3 Code does it.** T3 Code doesn't hold your credentials. Its README says it controls the Claude Code you already have installed and logged in (`claude auth login`), so usage draws on your subscription. I couldn't confirm from the README whether it spawns the CLI or uses the Agent SDK. I'm inferring that from "T3 Code can control them."

**What I found on Anthropic's policy:**
- Anthropic's terms bar using Free/Pro/Max OAuth tokens in other products or services, including the Agent SDK. Products built on Claude are expected to use API keys.
- A planned June 15, 2026 change would have moved programmatic usage into a separate credit pool. Anthropic's support page says that change is now paused.
- Right now, `claude -p` and Agent SDK usage still count against your subscription limits. I found nothing dated after the pause, so check [the support article](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15036540) before relying on this.

**What that means for AgentBisect.** The safe approach is to shell out to your own locally logged-in `claude -p` (headless, temperature isn't settable, JSON output) and never extract or reuse the OAuth token. That's the same pattern T3 Code uses on your own machine. It affects the build like this:
- **Fixer:** fits well, since it's already planned as headless Claude Code.
- **Target agent and evals:** `claude -p` would be the model backend. This works for a hackathon demo on your own account. The costs:
  - Each call carries Claude Code overhead.
  - You can't set temperature 0.
  - The 24 cases × repeats × commits will burn your 5-hour limit quickly.
- **Provider layer:** I'll build a swappable one. The default is `claude -p`, with an Anthropic API or Bedrock option behind an env var. The Bedrock credits might arrive, and a judge could ask you to run it on a key.

My recommendation is `claude -p` first, using the Haiku model for the target agent to stretch your limits, and switching to the API if you hit walls. Because of the temperature and rate-limit issues, the demo may need the cached-results fallback from your risks table.

**Housekeeping:**
- You pasted your neatlogs SDK key into chat. I'll put it only in a gitignored `.env` and never commit it. Consider rotating it after the hackathon.
- I haven't started building. I'll create the two public repos, set up `uv`, and start chunk 0 once you confirm.

1. There should be the history builder, which is the coding agent that writes the support agent's 20 commits. That's the Claude Code with `entire` on. This is a separate session from the one building the actual tool, the one actually building agent bisect, so that they don't know about each other.

- There's the fixer that writes the fix, which is a fresh agent that knows nothing about how the bugs were actually planted.

I'll delegate one worker to handle roles, model pinning, and judge enforcement (judge must be distinct from and not weaker than the agent model, enforced in code), then a second worker afterward to build a script that runs headless claude -p sessions per commit for the history builder.

**Policy.**
- Support article 15036540 (updated 2026-10-07) says `claude -p`, the Agent SDK and third-party apps still draw on subscription limits. Max and Team plans now also get monthly API credits that cover these.
- The legal page (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/legal-and-compliance) says developers building products should use API keys. It forbids routing requests through Free/Pro/Max credentials on behalf of users, and forbids collecting or storing Claude.ai credentials.
- It explicitly allows an end user to sign in to the unmodified Claude Code binary with their own subscription.
- It also says subscription limits assume "ordinary, individual usage".

**Policy risk.** A personal or hackathon tool that shells out to the user's own logged-in `claude`, with no token handling, matches the T3 pattern and the allowed case. The grey area is that hundreds of automated calls aren't "ordinary individual usage", so expect rate limits. Never extract or forward OAuth tokens. Never let judges or third parties use your subscription. Offer an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` provider for anyone else.

**Empirical results (claude 2.1.296).**
- Flags confirmed in `--help`: `--bare`, `--system-prompt`, `--tools`, `--disallowedTools`, `--strict-mcp-config`, `--setting-sources`, `--json-schema`, `--max-budget-usd`, `--no-session-persistence`, `--output-format`.
- **`--bare` fails here**: it returned "Not logged in", so bare mode does not use the subscription login. Don't use it.
- This call worked and cost about $0.0008: `claude -p ... --model claude-haiku-4-5 --output-format json --tools "" --system-prompt "..." --setting-sources "" --strict-mcp-config --no-session-persistence`.

- The JSON includes `usage`, `total_cost_usd`, `num_turns`, `is_error`, `result`, and a per-model `modelUsage` keyed by full model id.
- `modelUsage` also listed a second model, `claude-haiku-5-5`, with 1174 input tokens, so a side call is made under the hood. Count tokens from `modelUsage` rather than `usage`.
- I did not test `--max-turns`; it doesn't appear in the `--help` lines I grepped.

**Recommended Provider design.**
- Spawn `claude -p` per call with the flags above. Pin full model ids (`claude-haiku-4-5`, a Sonnet id). Record the id reported in `modelUsage`.
- Judge: use `--json-schema` for strict verdicts and `--tools ""`.
- Support agent: use in-process tools through the Agent SDK's custom MCP tools, or a stdio MCP server passed with `--mcp-config` plus `--strict-mcp-config`. Whitelist only those tool names with `--tools`. Check `init.tools` in `stream-json` output to confirm nothing leaks.
- Run in an empty cwd and set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY`-style isolation. Cap concurrency at 2-4 with retry and backoff on 429.
- Temperature: there is no flag, so you can't get temperature 0. Mitigate with a cache keyed on (prompt, model), repeat runs, and `--json-schema`.

**Bugs found and fixed** (commits `784068d` and the evidence commit, pushed)
1. The neatlogs SDK logs to stdout, which corrupted the demo harness's isolated-child JSON, so every case came back as an error. The eval env now sets `NEATLOGS_LOG_LEVEL=ERROR`, and the report parser tolerates leading log lines.
2. Repeats, workers, env file and baseline could not be set from the CLI. They now come from `AGENTBISECT_REPEATS`, `_MAX_REPEATS`, `_WORKERS`, `_ENV_FILE` and `_BASELINE`.
3. Fresh traces return `TRACE_PROCESSING`. Intake now retries, and an unreadable span lookup no longer fails it.

**Failed or unverified**
- Demo traces never finalize in neatlogs: each call is a separate trace with 0 spans. Trace-to-case mapping worked through the `case:` tag, but span divergence failed and there were no good-trace ids.
- The proxy cache is keyed on the prompt, so repeats are identical and R=2 adds no variance information.
- The judge was never run (no `--judge`), so I could not verify that the proxy honours the sonnet-5-5 pin. The agent model's pin was verified: results echoed `claude-haiku-5-5`.

Reports are in `/Users/jaxson/Downloads/codingprojects/agentbisect/evidence/report-6857f0b738.md` and `.html`, with notes appended to `BUILD_LOG.md`.

The first real investigation ran, and it exposed real problems. It also found a planted regression, though not the one the bad trace pointed at.

**What happened**
- **Setup:** good commit `2f49adb`, a bad `rw1` trace from HEAD, 3 cases × 2 repeats, about 160 CLI calls with no rate limiting.
- **Result:** AgentBisect named `59c8b10` (R2, the "verify replies with search_help" change) with low confidence. It flagged "multiple regressions likely", and the revert test failed to restore the pass rate.
- **Why that's a miss for this trace:** `rw1` failed on a cents amount (6400 vs 64.0), which points at R3 (`b0be626`) instead. AgentBisect didn't find R3, so I'd call this a partial result and not a success.

**Problems found**
1. **Smart bisect lost to plain:** 84 eval rounds over 14 commits, against 36 rounds over 6. It did cut graph context tokens (12.9k vs 26.4k), which is a real measured win.
2. **Repeats add no information:** the proxy cache keys on the prompt, so the second repeat is identical to the first. This also leaves flakiness handling untested.
3. **No span-level divergence:** each demo call lands in neatlogs as a separate trace with 0 spans. The planner therefore never used divergence to rank commits. It only worked through the `case:` tag.
4. **The judge never ran:** the Sonnet pin is unverified. The agent pin was verified.
5. **Overlapping regressions:** R2 broke the `rw` cases on its own (pass rate 0.33 at the culprit), so with R2 and R3 both active the search can't isolate R3 at HEAD. The tool noticed this, but it needs an answer.

**Fixed along the way** (pushed):
- Neatlogs logging was corrupting the eval JSON, so every case errored.
- CLI sampling settings are now configurable.
- Fresh traces no longer fail intake while they're still processing.

**Proposed next steps**
- **Make repeats real:** disable the proxy cache for repeats, or add a per-repeat salt.
- **Span-level tracing:** fix the demo's tracing so each run is one trace with spans.
- **Re-run smart vs plain** with those fixed. Smart should win on rounds if the divergence ranking works.
- **Handle overlapping regressions:** continue bisecting after a culprit is reverted, so each regression is found in turn.

Which should I do first, or all in that order? I'd also still run the skipped multi-reviewer pass on the whole MVP before chunks 10–15.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   - Build "AgentBisect" for the neatHack hackathon. It is `git bisect` for agent behavior: given a bad neatlogs trace, it finds the culprit commit, explains it via the Entire checkpoint intent, writes and verifies a fix, and reports (PR). The plan file is `/Users/jaxson/.t3/userdata/attachments/b4485d4e-7680-4b4c-9d6c-49b269b634a6-7907cc23-fb05-4601-80c3-ca209c94f914-md.md`.
   - The user asked me to figure out prerequisites, plan the build in chunks to avoid usage limits, verify with them, then build. They want sub-agents used to manage context bloat, and global CLAUDE.md compliance: one commit per unit, reviewer rounds, visual and local-server verification for UI work.
   - Role structure the user defined:
     1. History builder: a separate Claude Code session with `entire` on that writes the support agent's ~20 commits. It knows nothing of AgentBisect.
     2. Support agent (runtime "lab rat"): cheap model, Haiku, pinned.
     3. Eval judge: pinned, a smarter model than the agent (Sonnet) that follows the rubric.
     4. AgentBisect: the actual tool.
     5. Fixer: a fresh agent that knows nothing about how the bugs were planted.
   - Model backend: the user wants to avoid paying for an API key and use their Claude subscription "like T3 Code". Then they said: "look at T3 codes, source code… push the agent demo public after you fix the issues and then… do the investigation". All three are done.
   - Latest user instruction: "Continue" and the T3/push/investigate message. The next step is for me to relay the investigation results and propose follow-ups.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Smart bisect: trace divergence → `entire graph impact` → rank commits by Entire checkpoint intent. Plain bisect is the baseline. Tests run in git worktrees with K cases × R repeats and a flaky-confidence band.
   - neatlogs SDK (Python <3.14, 1.4.26): tags are process-wide, so one case runs per process. A neatlogs-cli (v0.2.1, installed at `~/.local/neatlogs-cli/bin/neatlogs`, profile `neatlogs-us`, host `https://app.neatlogs.com`) needs device login for reads. That login is now done.
   - Entire CLI: `entire checkpoint explain <sha> --full`, `entire checkpoint list`, `entire graph impact|diff|commit`. entire-graph works for Python. Checkpoints live under `refs/entire/checkpoints/*`.
   - Model pins: `AGENT_MODEL=claude-haiku-5-5` and `JUDGE_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5-5`. The judge guard refuses a judge equal to the agent or Haiku-tier. Results record agent_model and judge_model, and cross-model comparison is refused.
   - T3 Code approach: uses `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` pointed at the user's own installed `claude` binary. It does `claude auth status` and never handles tokens for inference. Anthropic policy allows a user's own login with the unmodified Claude Code, but not building products on subscription credentials or having third parties use it. The tool therefore keeps an API-key fallback.
   - `claude -p` proxy (llm_proxy.py): Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` server. It emulates tool use via `--json-schema`. Known-good flags: `--model`, `--output-format json`, `--tools ""`, `--system-prompt`, `--setting-sources ""`, `--strict-mcp-config`, `--no-session-persistence`, run in an empty cwd. `--bare` does not work with the subscription login. Temperature can't be set. Token counts come from `modelUsage`.
   - The `claude -p` CLI injects the logged-in user's ambient context (their email), which made the model refuse order lookups. The proxy now appends an ISOLATION_NOTICE to every system prompt.

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - `/Users/jaxson/Downloads/codingprojects/agentbisect` (public, pushed; ~100 tests passing). Files:
     - `ROLES.md`, `hackathon.md`, `BUILD_LOG.md`.
     - `evidence/ground_truth.json`: breaks and intent_for, moved out of the demo's cases.jsonl.
     - `agentbisect/models.py`: RegressionSpec, Plan, Candidate, CommitResult, BisectState, CulpritReport, FixAttempt, with to_dict/from_dict.
     - `state.py`: StateStore with atomic writes, a verdict cache keyed by (repo, sha, case, pinned models), and resume.
     - `runner.py`: worktree eval runner, EvalExecutor interface, SubprocessExecutor, skip on build failure, flaky escalation, and `eval_rounds`.
     - `tracing.py`: neatlogs tracing of AgentBisect itself.
     - `intake.py`: TraceSource (NeatlogsCliSource, FixtureSource), trace, detection and issue intake.
     - `bisect.py`: PlainStrategy, the engine, resume, and the multiple-regressions warning.
     - `planner.py`: SmartStrategy, `first_divergence`, `compare_strategies`.
     - `culprit.py`: CulpritReport and `fixer_brief`.
     - `verify.py`: `revert_test`. The fix verification hooks are not built yet (chunk 11).
     - `report.py`: Markdown and HTML reports, dry-run `open_pr`.
     - `llm_proxy.py`: the claude-CLI proxy, including `--debug-dump DIR`.
     - `cli.py`: commands investigate (`--strategy smart|plain`, `--intake-only`, `--llm-proxy auto|URL|off`), intake, resume, status, compare, report, llm-proxy. `watch` is still a stub.
     - Env vars: `AGENTBISECT_REPEATS`, `_MAX_REPEATS`, `_WORKERS`, `_ENV_FILE`, `_BASELINE`.
     - Investigation reports: `evidence/report-6857f0b738.md` and `.html`.
   - `/Users/jaxson/Downloads/codingprojects/support-agent-demo` (public, pushed, HEAD `f7d82b7`):
     - `agent/` (loop.py, prompt.py, provider.py, tracing.py), `tools/impl.py`, `data/` (orders.json, articles.json), `evals/` (cases.jsonl, harness.py, judge.py, models.py, reference.py, README.md), and tests.
     - History: brief 1 `1b40b27`, brief 6 (R1, cancel_order) `ec19917`, brief 11 (R2) `59c8b10`, brief 16 (R3) `b0be626`, brief 20 `5cee99b`; fix commits `432b083`, `d9b1680`, `f7d82b7`. Brief 10 is `2f49adb`, used as the good commit.
   - `/Users/jaxson/.agentbisect-private/` (outside both repos): `briefs.jsonl`, `run_builder.sh`, `drive.sh`, `ground_truth_commits.json`. Only the history builder and final scoring may use it.
   - `.env` files hold the neatlogs key and project ID `110108af-1737-47ee-8494-cf482d13defd`. Both are gitignored.

4. Errors and fixes:
   - Usage limit (HTTP 429) killed the chunk 5 worker. No partial work was left, and the user reset it themselves. I re-ran chunk 5.
   - The neatlogs SDK needs Python <3.14, so the projects are pinned to 3.13.
   - The SDK has no `temperature` argument, so temp 0 goes through `extra_body`. This is untested against the live API.
   - The proxy's first tool prompt made Haiku claim it had no tools. I rewrote the prompt, and tool calls then worked.
   - The `os1` refusal at HEAD came from `claude -p` injecting the user's email into the prompt. Fixed with ISOLATION_NOTICE (agentbisect `318146d`); HEAD passed 9/9 on os1–os3 afterwards.

## boardui
BoardUI is a React + Tailwind CSS v4 design system (Next.js first) with free components and paid Pro components/templates. This server installs component source directly into the user's project — no terminal needed.

Typical flow:
1. In a project without BoardUI, call init_boardui once (installs Tailwind v4 + runtime deps, writes styles/ and utils/).
2. Discover with list_components; read source/props with get_component; get working code with get_usage_examples.
3. Install with install_components — it writes the files and installs npm deps.

Component names are exact — when unsure, call list_components instead of guessing.

## RTL Support

BoardUI supports Arabic, Hebrew, and other right-to-left languages across free components, Pro blocks, and templates. The same source handles RTL and LTR; there is no RTL CLI flag or separate component version.

1. Read get_component and get_usage_examples for the free `direction` item. Install it with install_components (stdio), or write its source and dependencies yourself (read-only HTTP). CLI equivalent: `npx boardui@latest add direction`.
2. Wrap the app with DirectionProvider using an explicit BCP 47 locale: `ar` for Arabic, `he` for Hebrew, `en-US` for English. Set matching `lang` and `dir` on `<html>` for a full-app RTL layout. CSS dir alone does not configure React Aria keyboard navigation, calendars, or portalled menus.

```tsx
import { DirectionProvider } from "@/components/foundations/direction/direction";

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
      <body>
        <DirectionProvider locale="ar">{children}</DirectionProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

3. Use logical styles such as ps/pe, ms/me, start/end, and text-start/text-end. Mirror navigation arrows and drawer motion; preserve physical coordinates for charts, canvas, and decorative art. Custom portals should carry `dir={useDirection()}` on their root. Nest DirectionProvider for mixed-language regions.
4. Keep email addresses, URLs, OTP digits, and code LTR; isolate mixed text with bdi or dir=auto. Choose fonts with Arabic or Hebrew coverage and avoid extra letter spacing for Arabic. Translate application labels and accessible names in the application's translation layer; use Intl for dates, numbers, and currencies. Optional `template-copy` supplies TemplateCopyProvider for translating template display copy. Chinese (`zh-CN`) remains LTR.
5. For older installations, refresh the provider, component source, shared dependencies, and global styles. Preserve customizations before using overwrite. Pro updates use the licensed CLI or updated source downloads.

Setup and live Arabic/Hebrew examples: https://www.boardui.com/rtl

Design rules (always apply when writing UI in a BoardUI project): style with BoardUI's semantic Tailwind tokens, never raw palette classes or hex — text via text-text-primary/-secondary/-tertiary, surfaces via bg-background-*-default/-hover, borders via border-border-* and border-separator-border, icons via text-foreground-icon-*. Type uses composite utilities (text-title-2-medium, text-headline-medium, text-body-medium, ...) that set size/weight/line-height together — never rebuild them from text-sm font-medium. Dark mode flips tokens automatically via the .dark class; never hardcode dark: colors. Merge classes with cx() from @/utils/cx (or the utils alias configured in boardui.json); icons from @remixicon/react as component references. init_boardui installs these rules as always-on files (AGENTS.md + .cursor/rules/boardui.mdc) so they survive beyond this session; install_rules adds them to an already initialized project.

Monorepos/custom aliases: put boardui.json next to the destination package's package.json, and pass that package as projectDir. Installs read its paths/aliases and keep npm dependencies in that package. Pass projectDir to get_component and get_usage_examples too for matching source and examples. Package exports and each consuming app's stylesheet/Tailwind setup must already be wired by th… [truncated]

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

Ghostfeed agent API. Workflow guidance is available through list_skills/get_skill, native skill resources and matching MCP prompts; load the relevant skill when composing a workflow. Resolve workspace names through list_workspaces and Brand names through list_brands; these identities are distinct and must not be treated as interchangeable. When available in the host, use the matching render_* app tool to show the avatar builder, inspirations, generations, crop editor, or image/video results. Without App tools, use returned media and dashboard URLs. Do not build a replacement Ghostfeed UI or call the Ghostfeed HTTP API from generated presentation code.

Recipe/setup slashes: get_preset_instructions before other workflows; unambiguous model slashes: models_explore; unknowns: resolve. Higgsfield Genjutsu routes through generate_video: motion transfer -> hf_mult_motion_control; object replacement -> hf_mult_replace_object. Without an explicit preset recipe, for multi-step videos call get_workflow_instructions first (with no argument). For clip edits call get_workflow_instructions with { workflow: "ad-multiplier" } first. AI Influencer: ai_influencer_prepare then ai_influencer_generate. Character sheets: call get_workflow_instructions with { workflow: "character-sheet" }; websites/apps/games: call get_workflow_instructions with { workflow: "website-builder-flow" }. Character sheets require explicit requests. Bundled files: get_workflow_bundle_file. For AI Influencer chat creation, use ai_influencer_get_options for explicit traits, ai_influencer_list_presets for examples, or ai_influencer_get_settings with job_id for an existing sheet. ai_influencer_prepare returns design and price without generation. Preserve references and seed; use randomize=false for exact settings. Pass prepared params unchanged to ai_influencer_generate with max_credits at the quote or a lower user budget. Existing creation intent permits proceeding within budget; preview-only requests must stop after preparation. For explicit free-only intent, require known available free_gens_remaining and use_free_gens=true with max_credits=0; never fall back to credits. For variants, prepare each sheet and respect total count and aggregate budget. The generator opens an auto-updating widget for progress and the completed sheet. Wait with jobs_wait (timeout_seconds <= 15); do not duplicate the display with show_generation_by_ids or job_display unless explicitly requested. Offer Genjutsu animation afterward unless declined; require agreement and selection of the exact completed character before get_presets source=genjutsu category=genjutsu with initial_inputs.character_sheet=[{id:job_id,type:image_job}]. Opening that gallery does not authorize video submission. If chat creation is unavailable, report it without silently switching to generic image generation or the builder UI. Multiple independent generations: batch tools, jobs_wait, then one show_generation_by_ids. Use generate_3d to turn an image into a 3D GLB mesh. When unsure which model fits, call models_explore(action:'recommend') before calling a generate_* tool. Use virality_predictor when the user asks to predict video virality or analyze engagement, attention, audience response, retention risk, hook strength, or creative performance. For other existing-asset edits use upscale_image/video, outpaint_image, reframe, remove_background, relight_image, or motion_control (single-character Kling recast). For voice creation in Apps UI-capable clients, call create_voice … [truncated]

## slide-studio
First call list_editors and use the registered local browser tab. Never open or connect CarouselBot through a sandboxed agent browser. If no editor is listed, retry briefly because browser reconnection is automatic, then ask the user to open https://carousel.bot in their normal browser and click Connect AI. Companion compatibility and reconnects are automatic. Do not parallel-retry an action that reports an unsupported internal action; retry once after list_editors so automatic recovery can finish. Never restart a healthy companion for a transient editor disconnect. Before edits call get_design_guidance, then begin_edit_session; pass editSessionId to every edit and end it in cleanup. Parallel workers can share the same browser tab and project; sessions track targets without exclusive locks. Use render_slide to inspect actual pixels.

content.text:
Fix: bisect on a failure signature, not a case.

Intake: pull the specific failing check out of the bad trace, e.g. refund amount: expected 64.0, got 6400.
Bisect: at each commit, only ask “does this failure reproduce?” Budget failures from R2 don’t count.
Revert test: revert the culprit on HEAD and check that this signature disappears.
Overlapping regressions (problem 5): group all failing checks at HEAD into signatures and bisect each one separately. R1, R2 and R3 each get found on their own. Pitch it as: “it separates overlapping regressions by failure signature.”
The other four

Problem 1: 
Fix it with weighted bisect: rank commits as before, but pick the commit that splits the probability in half instead of trying the top candidate first.
With good ranking it beats plain; with no information it degrades to plain bisect. That way it can never take more rounds than plain bisect.
The failure signature also fixes the ranking. An amount bug sends entire-graph to the refund and amount code, which points straight at R3’s commit.

Problem 3: 


Wrap each eval case in one parent trace, with tool calls as child spans. Make sure neatlogs instrumentation is on. Check neatlogs’ SDK reference for the trace-context API.
This is the top priority. 

Problem 2: repeats add no information.

Key the cache on (commit, case, repeat), or skip the cache for repeats.
Since you’re at temperature 0 with deterministic checks, default to one repeat. Add repeats only when a result is borderline or judge-based. That alone cuts rounds a lot.
To actually exercise flakiness handling, make one mocked tool time out 30% of the time on purpose. That also gives you a natural recovery run.

Problem 4: the judge never ran. That’s fine for deterministic cases. Make one smoke-test call so the Sonnet pin shows up in a trace. Low priority.

Also add a concurrency limit and backoff on model calls. 160 unthrottled calls will eventually hit rate limits, and when that happens it’s more recovery evidence.

Keep: the 51% cut in context tokens (12.9k vs 26.4k) is a real, measured Entire win. Put it in evidence/ now.

# Large multi-feature tasks

When a request is big — multiple features, or a large ask that naturally splits into independent
pieces of work — do not implement it as one monolithic pass. Split it into separate commits, one
per feature/unit of work, and drive each unit through this graph-engineering framework using the
Agent tool:

```
Task -> Planner -> Worker -> [Reviewer 1, Reviewer 2, ... Reviewer N] -> Synthesise -> Pass?
                     ^                                                        |
                     |-------------------- feedback (no) ---------------------|
                                                                               |
                                                                          (yes) -> commit -> next unit
```

- **Planner**: breaks the overall ask into an ordered list of commit-sized units of work (a
  Plan Reviewer can review the plan itself before execution starts; route its feedback back to
  the Planner and send a summary of plan feedback to the user).
- **Worker**: a resident agent (kept alive across the reviewer round for a given unit) that
  implements one unit of work.
- **Reviewers (1..N)**: spawn multiple reviewer agents in parallel against the Worker's output —
  e.g. correctness, simplification/efficiency, and test coverage as separate reviewer passes.
  These can be ephemeral (fresh agent per round).
- **Synthesise**: reconcile the reviewers' findings into one set of required changes.
- **Pass? gate**: if synthesised feedback has no blocking issues, finalize and commit that unit
  with its own commit message, then move to the next planned unit. If it fails, send the
  synthesised feedback back to the Worker as another round on the same unit (don't restart from
  the Planner unless the feedback reveals the plan itself was wrong).

Net effect: one commit per feature/unit, each vetted by multiple reviewer passes before it lands,
rather than a single large uncommitted or unreviewed diff at the end.

## Verifying UI work: visual recreation (the main way to verify)

For any unit that changes UI, the primary verification is a **visual recreation**: render the real
components with mock data and look at a screenshot. Typecheck and unit tests are necessary but do not
count as verifying how it looks. Workers should do this before reporting, and I re-do it (or open the
image for the user) when the user asks to see it.

1. Add a **temporary** preview route (e.g. `apps/web/app/zz-preview/page.tsx`) that imports the real
   components and renders them with realistic mock props: populated, empty, capped/failed, long
   names/links. Put context around them (page background, a mock frame for panels/drawers that need a
   session or client state) but never reimplement the component itself.
2. Start the dev server in the background with dummy env vars the app needs to boot (e.g.
   `CONVEX_URL=https://dummy.convex.cloud CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY=x NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 bunx next dev -p <port>`),
   wait for "Ready", and `curl` the route for a 200.
3. Screenshot with headless Chrome, not the preview MCP tools (those time out):
   `"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless=new --disable-gpu --hide-scrollbars --force-device-scale-factor=2 --virtual-time-budget=6000 --window-size=<w>,<h> --screenshot=/tmp/<name>.png <url>`
   Take a wide desktop shot and a narrow one. Headless Chrome enforces a minimum window width, so a
   narrow shot can come out horizontally clipped; for true 320px checks render inside a 320px-wide
   iframe or measure element widths, and say so rather than treating clipping as a bug.
4. **Read the PNG** (the Read tool shows images) and actually look at it: hierarchy, spacing, truncation,
   overflow, alignment, tap targets, copy. Report what was seen versus what was not verified
   (hover/focus states, real clipboard/share, animations, Safari-only behavior, the real page behind auth).
5. For the user, `open` the desktop screenshot (copy it to `~/Downloads/<name>.png` first) since they
   can't see tool-output images.
6. **Clean up before committing**: stop the dev server (`pkill -f "next dev -p <port>"`), delete the
   preview route, temp public files and stray `.next` artifacts, and confirm `git status` shows only
   intended changes. Never commit a preview route or mocks.

# Mandatory visual + local-server verification (every agent, every run)

Applies to any task that changes code a user can see or that the running app depends on. No unit of
work is "done" until both of these have happened and been reported:

1. **Run it against the local server.** Start the real dev server (and `npx convex dev` when Convex
   code changed) in this worktree, wait for "Ready", and exercise the changed path end to end: `curl`
   the route for the expected status and hit changed API routes. A passing typecheck/lint/build alone
   does not count.
2. **Verify visually with a screenshot.** Follow the visual-recreation steps above (headless Chrome,
   wide + narrow shot), then Read the PNG and look at it. For pages behind auth, use a temporary
   preview route with mock data. Non-UI changes still get a screenshot of the affected page to prove
   nothing regressed.
3. **Report** what was seen, what was not verified (hover/focus, auth-gated pages, animations), and
   the screenshot path. If the server can't boot (e.g. missing env vars), say so explicitly and fix
   the env first (see below); never claim success without having run it.
4. Clean up (stop the server, delete preview routes/temp files) before committing.

Env vars: each worktree needs its own copy of the gitignored `.env*` files. If `.env.local` is
missing in the current worktree, symlink it from the canonical copy at `~/.config/avian/.env.local`
(`ln -s ~/.config/avian/.env.local .env.local`) before starting the server.

entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

entries.name: WebSearch
entries.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. - "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

Work in /Users/jaxson/Downloads/codingprojects/agentbisect (Python, uv, ~100 tests; read BUILD_LOG.md, ROLES.md, agentbisect/{models,runner,intake,bisect,planner,culprit,verify,cli,llm_proxy}.py first). Make ONE commit per unit below, each with tests passing (uv run pytest), commit messages ending with: Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>. Push to origin main at the end.

Background: first real investigation (evidence/report-6857f0b738.md) bisected on "case fails" and named R2 for a trace that actually failed on R3 (refund amount expected 64.0 got 6400); R2 budget failures also fail the rw cases, so overlapping regressions confused it. Smart bisect used 84 rounds vs plain 36. Repeats were identical because the proxy cache is keyed on the prompt.

Units:
U1 evidence: write evidence/entire-context-savings.md recording the measured 51% context-token cut (graph context 12.9k vs raw 26.4k tokens) with how it was measured, from the existing report and state data. Commit.
U2 failure signature (biggest): bisect on a failure signature, not a case. Intake extracts the specific failing check from the bad trace/eval result (e.g. check=refund_amount, expected 64.0, got 6400) into a FailureSignature (add to models.py with to_dict/from_dict; resume-safe). Evals per commit record per-check failures; the bisect predicate becomes "does THIS signature reproduce?" — other failures (e.g. budget failures from R2) count as pass for this signature. revert_test verifies that signature disappears when culprit is reverted on HEAD. Overlapping regressions: group all failing checks at HEAD into signatures and bisect each separately (new `investigate --all-signatures` or default when several are present), producing one culprit per signature; report should say it separates overlapping regressions by failure signature. Verdict cache key must include the signature or per-check results. Also feed the signature into the planner's ranking (amount/refund keywords -> entire graph impact on matching code).
U3 weighted bisect: SmartStrategy picks the commit that splits the cumulative candidate probability mass in half (weighted by rank scores), not the top candidate; with uniform scores it degrades to exactly plain bisect, so rounds(smart) <= rounds(plain) always. Add a property test for that bound.
U4 repeats/cache: key the verdict/proxy cache on (commit, case, repeat); default repeats = 1; escalate to extra repeats only when a result is borderline (flaky band) or judge-based. Keep AGENTBISECT_REPEATS override. Make sure repeats actually differ (include repeat index in cache key / salt, not in the model prompt semantic content if avoidable).
U5 throttling: concurrency limit and exponential backoff with jitter on model calls in llm_proxy (and 429/overloaded handling), configurable via env (AGENTBISECT_MODEL_CONCURRENCY default 4); log backoff events into state so they can be cited as recovery evidence. Unit-test with a fake failing backend.
U6 judge smoke test: add `agentbisect judge-smoke` (or script) that makes one Sonnet judge call through the proxy against the pinned JUDGE_MODEL and prints the model recorded; don't run live more than once, and only if the proxy works. Low priority; skip live run if it costs much.

Per CLAUDE.md I need reviewer rounds: after each unit's worker pass is done, spawn parallel reviewer sub-agents (correctness, simplification, test coverage), fix blocking findings, then commit. Keep the final report brief: commits, test count, what was and was not verified live. Update BUILD_LOG.md.

<result>Gaps are ordered by how likely they are to hide a real bug. The first three are probably actual bugs, so write those tests first. I read the diff and `tests/test_signature.py` but did not run the suite or any new tests.

**P0: likely real bugs**

1. **The CLI never runs siblings if the primary fails.**
   - In `cli.py`, `code = code or _run_one(store, sib, meta)` short-circuits once `code` is non-zero. Siblings are created and announced but never executed.
   - No test calls `main(["investigate"...])` with siblings at all.
   - Minimal test: monkeypatch `_run_one` to return 1 for the primary. Assert that sibling states exist and that `_run_one` was called for each. Add a second case where the primary returns 0, and assert there is one culprit per signature and that `resume` does not spawn siblings.

2. **An explicit `--signature` or a trace-supplied signature disables sibling discovery.**
   - `_discover_signature` returns early, so `metrics["signatures"]` is never set. `spawn_siblings` then returns `[]`, and `--all-signatures` silently does nothing.
   - `test_explicit_signature_skips_discovery` only asserts `"signatures" not in metrics`, so it locks that behaviour in rather than questioning it.
   - Minimal test: investigate with an explicit signature and `all_signatures=True` over an `OverlapExec` history. Decide whether siblings are expected, then assert it.
   - A related issue is that the CLI sets `st.spec.signature` without resetting `signatures_discovered`. A second `--signature` on a resumed investigation keeps stale `metrics["signatures"]`. Add a test for that too.

3. **A partial or mismatched signature key matches nothing.**
   - `--signature call_args` or `--signature judge:x` never equals the emitted keys, which look like `call_args:tool.arg` or `judge`. Every commit then reads as a pass and the bisect reports "bad end not reproducing" or a bogus culprit.
   - Minimal test: set `signature_from_key("call_args")` with `OverlapExec`. Assert the investigation fails with an explicit "signature does not reproduce at bad" message instead of a culprit. The same test covers a trace-supplied `check:` tag that does not fire at the bad end.

4. **Discovery at a bad end with no signatures.**
   - Cover two cases: a build skip at `bad`, and all runs erroring at `bad`. In both, `failure_signatures` is empty.
   - `_discover_signature` still sets `signatures_discovered=True` and appends the "whole-case pass rate" warning.
   - Minimal test: a `BUILD_CASE` skip at the bad sha, and an executor that returns errors. Assert a clean failure or fallback, a single warning, no crash, and `signature is None`.

5. **Resume mid-discovery.**
   - If the executor raises during the discovery step, `in_flight` is set but `signatures_discovered` is not.
   - Minimal test: an executor that raises on its Nth call. Call `run_investigation` and catch the error. Then call `resume_investigation` with a working executor. Assert that discovery runs exactly once, the step and `eval_rounds` accounting is consistent, and the final culprit is correct.

**P1: untested wiring**

6. **The planner using the signature.**
   - Only the `symbol_hints` and `symptom_text` helpers are tested. `Planner.plan` is not.
   - Minimal test: put `spec.signature = AMOUNT` on a state and stub `locate` and the intent scorer to record their arguments. Assert that:
     - hints contain `issue_refund` and `_tool_issue_refund`;
     - the symptom contains "unit conversion";
     - divergence hints are merged and de-duplicated;
     - an explicit `self.symbol_hints` override still wins.
   - Also test with no signature, where behaviour must match the old path.

7. **Cache v2 isolation.**
   - Minimal test: write a v1-style cache file keyed `sha|case|agent|judge` with `passes` and `fails` and no `check_fails`. Load it and call `evaluate_commit`.
   - Assert the old entry is ignored (the runs are re-executed) and nothing raises `KeyError` or `TypeError`.
   - Also assert that the `__build__` skip is stored and read under the v2 key.

8. **Per-signature tallies and flakiness.**
   - Minimal test: one case where run 1 fails with `AMOUNT` and run 2 passes. Assert that a signature-filtered `_tally` marks it flaky and doubles the repeats.
   - A second sibling evaluation with a different signature must hit the same cache entries with zero extra runs. Assert this on `executor.runs`.
   - Add a case where a run fails only with `BUDGET` and the signature is `AMOUNT`. Assert it counts as a pass.

9. **`pick_primary` ordering.**
   - Minimal unit test over a set of signatures: a deterministic check beats `budget`, which beats `judge`. Fall back to the first when `bad_case` is in no signature. Return `None` for empty input. Use `bad_case=None`.
   - Also unit-test `group_signatures` with a case that has `runs=0` and with multiple cases.

**P2: parser and edge cases**

10. **`failures_of_result` and `_call_args_failures`.**
    - Minimal parametrized test covering:
      - budget reason mentioning both steps and tokens;
      - budget fail naming neither, which defaults to steps;
      - `judge.passed=False`;
      - `status=fail` with no checks, which gives `case_fail`;
      - `symptom_text` returning `""` for `case_fail`;
      - a regex reason with nested braces such as `{'items': {'a': 1}}`, which hits the `literal_eval` fallback key `call_args:tool`;
      - two failed `call_args` checks;
      - a `0.004` versus `0.006` boundary on the numeric tolerance.

11. **Intake without trace hints.**
    - `test_intake_sets_bad_case_and_trace_signature` covers only the with-hints path.
    - Minimal test: a trace with no `failed_checks`. Assert that `spec.signature is None`, `bad_case == case.id`, and the "taken from the bad end's eval results" note is present. Then run the end-to-end `OverlapExec` investigation from that spec.

12. **`spawn_siblings` edge cases.**
    - Minimal test: when `st.spec.signature` is set but `st.spec.signature.key` is also in `signatures`, skip it (already covered).
    - Add the case where `signatures` is empty and the case where `signature_siblings` already holds an entry for a key. Assert that siblings copy `bad_case`, `cases`, `strategy` and `source`, and that the sibling's signature `cases` is restricted to where it fires.

13. **Report and verify.**
    - Minimal test: a report with a signature but no siblings, and with a sibling that has no `culprit`. Assert it renders without a `KeyError`.
    - Minimal test: `revert_test` with `signature=None` keeps the old behaviour and does not add `details["signature"]`.</result>

content.text:
`rw1`–`rw4` are four scripted customer messages. Each one asks for a refund the agent should grant, and the eval checks that the agent does it correctly. "rw" stands for "refund within policy".

| Case | Customer says | The agent should |
|---|---|---|
| `rw1` | "Order 1007 arrived broken, I want my money back" | Look up order 1007, then issue a refund of **$64.00** |
| `rw2` | "The backpack from order 1015 is defective. Please refund it." | Look up order 1015, then refund **$79.99** |
| `rw3` | "The speaker in order 1031 doesn't work. Refund me please." | Look up order 1031, then refund **$59.00** |
| `rw4` | "Please refund my order 1060, the notebooks were damaged" | Look up order 1060, then refund **$36.00** (held out) |

The checks are the same in every case:
- **Tool order:** the first tool call is `lookup_order`.
- **Required calls:** `lookup_order` and `issue_refund` are both called, and `issue_refund` is called exactly once.
- **Forbidden calls:** the agent must not call `escalate_to_human` or `cancel_order`.
- **Refund amount:** the refund amount argument must equal the dollar value above.
- **Reply text:** the reply must mention the right dollar amount, and must not contain the cents form (such as "6400").

`rw4` is held out. The fixer never sees it, so it tests whether a fix generalizes.

The failure in the investigation was the `rw1` cents check. The agent issued a refund of 6400 where 64.0 was expected, which is the amount bug planted in R3. The `rw` cases also fail whenever R2 is active, because R2 breaks the "verify with `search_help`" step. That overlap is why plain "case fails" bisecting blamed R2. Bisecting on the specific failing check, such as "refund amount 6400 vs 64.0", is the fix I've asked the worker to build.
