The AgentBisect worker finished all six units and pushed them to origin main (`37c9144`). 141 tests pass. The demo worker is still investigating why neatlogs shows the new traces as empty.

**What landed**
- **51% evidence:** the context-token cut is written up in `evidence/entire-context-savings.md`. It is 12,869 vs 26,420 planner tokens, estimated from bytes/4 over one range.
- **Failure signatures:**
  - Bisect now asks whether the specific failing check still reproduces, so R2's budget failures no longer count against an R3 hunt.
  - The revert test uses the same check.
  - By default, extra signatures at HEAD each get their own sibling investigation, and `--signature KEY` forces one.
- **Weighted bisect:** it probes the commit that splits the ranking mass in half. With no ranking information it matches plain bisect exactly, and it never exceeds plain's worst-case round count.
- **Repeats and cache:** the cache is keyed on (commit, case, repeat). Repeats default to 1, and extras run only for borderline or judge-graded results.
- **Throttling:** model calls have a concurrency limit (default 4) and exponential backoff with jitter. Backoff events are saved to the investigation state and shown in the report.
- **Judge smoke test:** I ran `agentbisect judge-smoke` live once. It recorded `claude-sonnet-5-5`, which matches the pin.

**What is not verified**
- None of the signature, weighted-bisect or repeat paths has run against the real demo repo. They were only tested with fake executors on throwaway git repos.
- The backoff code was only tested against a fake failing `claude`, not a real rate limit.
- U6 had no reviewer round. The U2 review fixes landed in a separate commit after U2 was committed. The new tests and the U5 fixes were not re-reviewed.
- Real neatlogs traces don't carry failing-check detail, so the signature comes from the bad end's eval results when the trace has no hint.
- Spans: both new demo traces I read back show `dlq` with 0 spans, even though the parent span name arrived. The demo worker is looking for the cause.

Once the span fix lands, the next step is a real re-run on the demo. I'd use a good commit before R1 so all three regressions are in range, and run smart bisect against plain on it. That would show whether the signature, weighted-bisect and repeat changes work together. I'll wait for the demo worker first, because span divergence is what lets smart beat plain.

The demo worker found no fix to make. It traced the dead-lettering to neatlogs' backend, not our code.

**What it found**
- **SDK side is clean:** it reported 0 export failures and 0 drops.
- **Not shape-dependent:** the backend finalized one shape, a root `WORKFLOW` span with one `TOOL` child. A later exact repeat of that same shape went to `dlq`, so the shape isn't the cause.
- **Not caused by our code:** it reproduced the failures with bare scripts that make no model calls and use none of the demo code.
- **Not caused by attribute types:** string, int and JSON attributes all behaved the same.
- **Not an overall outage:** older single-span traces finalized earlier in the day, around 21:23 to 21:24.
- **Repro:** `/tmp/bis4.py C2` and `/tmp/bis.py`. Several of the test traces never ingested at all (NOT_FOUND).

The demo's tracing in `67f3521` (`support_case` > `agent.run` > `tool:*` and model calls) is correct on the SDK side. I couldn't confirm it shows up server-side, because no multi-span trace has finalized.

**What this means for AgentBisect.** Span-level divergence can't be demonstrated live until neatlogs fixes finalization. The signature path doesn't depend on spans, so the main investigation is unaffected. I'd rather not claim span divergence as working in the pitch without a trace that finalizes.

**Next steps**
- **Report to neatlogs:** the trace ids and repro need to go to the neatlogs team, and I can draft that message. Since this is a hackathon sponsor, they may be able to dead-letter-check quickly.
- **Re-run the investigation:** I'd run it again with a good commit before R1, using signatures, weighted bisect and single repeats. That would show whether the whole pipeline finds R1, R2 and R3 separately. It's the main thing still unverified.
- **Fixture fallback:** if neatlogs can't fix finalization in time, I can use a recorded span fixture for the divergence demo and label it as such.

I'd start with the re-run. Should I go ahead, or would you rather draft the neatlogs message first?

# neatlogs: multi-span traces finalize as `dlq` with 0 spans

Project `110108af-1737-47ee-8494-cf482d13defd` (neatlogs-us, https://app.neatlogs.com). Python SDK 1.4.26, Python 3.13, 2026-10-10.

## Summary

Traces with more than one span end in `finalizationStatus: "dlq"` with `spansCount: 0`. The SDK reports 0 export failures and 0 drops (`get_delivery_diagnostics()`), so the spans leave the client. The backend then leaves the trace `pending` for about 7 minutes and dead-letters it.

It is not shape-dependent: the same code produced a finalized trace once and `dlq` twice afterwards. Single-span traces from earlier the same day (21:23 to 21:24 UTC) finalized fine.

## Minimal repro

A bare script: one `WORKFLOW` span with one `TOOL` child via `neatlogs.trace()`, then `flush()` and `shutdown()`. No model calls and no application code. Run it 3 times.

| Run | Trace id | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `af41536424d272b3696bdc616e40143e` | finalized, 2 spans |
| 2 | `99a3a8d5ad662f4bac4cbc47e964ffc5` | `dlq`, 0 spans |
| 3 | `a25f8e0c33f84eaa716ac6eab355050e` | `dlq`, 0 spans |

Other variants (all `dlq`, 0 spans, or never ingested):

- `WORKFLOW` + 2 `TOOL` siblings: `c29bcec815dab4068db3766f06beab6d`, `fadd81a6bba43dc8a84215164a66c0d2`
- Nested or 3+ spans: `ed094ad96d4c040d4ef645f5f01d633a`, `75ad436dc68f7541fa76743668031d99`, `2e1c41856ca841bc5d6d2d9605b29c26`
- Real app runs (`support_case` parent with `tool:*` children and wrapped model calls): `5ad517664ed4dbd323aaf32526ceacbf` (dlq), `dca67a22affcc988c9af943794aae4fe` (dlq), `f502464ebbce39102545d28ddae32435` (NOT_FOUND on read)
- Never ingested (NOT_FOUND): `2efe8dec27efcadc3bce6466972b912b`, `66be775a76c204969e15d8f947d2a10e`, `a155af5daf3848ccf7bc667ea06874c1`, `91b8c7dfc660f1032c34685f19cae705`, `353ec64dcc8643d324c44031ada21bc5`

## Ruled out on our side

- Attribute types (string, int, JSON-encoded): no difference.
- Tags (empty vs non-empty): no difference.
- Wrapped model calls (`neatlogs.wrap`): failures reproduce without them.
- SDK export: 0 failures, 0 drops.

## What we need

1. Why these traces were dead-lettered (backend log or DLQ reason for the ids above).
2. Whether there is a known SDK or ingest constraint for nested or multi-span traces that we are missing.
3. A way to re-drive the dlq traces, if possible.

## Why it matters

AgentBisect (neatHack) uses neatlogs traces to find where a failing agent run first diverges from a good one. It needs span-level data (tool calls with args and results) and cannot get it while multi-span traces dead-letter.

<result>I found three blocking issues and one minor one. I read the diff and the consuming code but didn't run any tests or the harness.

**Blocking**

1. **A signature given as `budget:steps|tokens` no longer matches anything.** `agentbisect/signature.py:76-77` now emits `budget:steps@<cat>` whenever the harness result has a `category`. `Runner._tally` (`agentbisect/runner.py:~385`) and `_signatures` compare `check_fails` by exact key.
   - Affected: `--signature budget:steps` (`signature_from_key`), a `check:budget:steps` trace tag, and any `spec.signature` already saved in an investigation state.
   - Result: fails is 0 at every commit, so the bad end evaluates as good and the bisect errors out or goes wrong.
   - Resume: cached `check_fails` and `check_info` from before this change also still use the old keys. The verdict cache is keyed commit/case/repeat with no key-format version. A resumed investigation that has `budget:steps` in its spec therefore sees 0 fails.
   - Fix: match budget keys by prefix, or by `check == "budget"` plus the key with the `@cat` suffix stripped, in `_tally`. Alternatively version or migrate the cache.

2. **Single-run noise can still enter the signature list from the confirm pass.** `agentbisect/bisect.py:~168` keeps `x.fails >= 2 or x.key not in weak_keys`.
   - A key that first appears in the confirm re-run (so it isn't in `weak_keys`) with `fails == 1` is kept as a real signature.
   - This is the same noise the change is meant to drop. The filter should be `x.fails >= 2` for every key that had `fails < 2` in either pass. In practice that means dropping the `weak_keys` clause and applying `fails >= 2` to every key in `everything`.
   - The same line can also wrongly drop a key that was strong in the first pass. The first pass saw it fail in the cases it ran. `signatures_at` recomputes over all of `st.spec.cases` from the cache, so it should still count them, but nothing tests this.

3. **`pick_primary` can now bisect a signature from the wrong case.** At `bisect.py:~168-173`, if the bad trace's own signature is dropped as unconfirmed, `pick_primary` falls back to `sigs[0]` from some other case. The code then bisects that unrelated failure silently. If the bad trace's case has no confirmed signature, at least add a warning, or fall back to whole-case pass rate.

**Minor, not blocking**

- `FailureSignature.detail` now carries `steps@cat`. `symptom_text` (`agentbisect/signature.py:156`) feeds that token into the planner's intent scoring, where it is noise. `symbol_hints` is unaffected.
- No `budget:` parsing exists in the planner, report or culprit code, so there is nothing else to break there.

**Checked and fine**

- `runner.cfg.repeats` is mutated and restored in `try/finally`, and `RunnerConfig` is not frozen.
- The confirm pass reuses cached runs because the cache is keyed by run index. A crash and resume re-runs at most the unfinished cases.
- `--all-categories` doesn't leak held-out cases.</result>

<note>This agent stopped with background work of its own still running. It may resume on its own when that work completes or reports, and the same task-id notifies again if it does; the result below may be interim.</note>
<result>Only R3 came out cleanly; R1 and R2 did not get their own culprit with a passing revert test. I pushed everything to origin main (HEAD `4f05452`).

**Setup:** good `1b40b27`, bad `f7d82b7`, DEMO_FLAKE=0, haiku agent and sonnet judge through the llm-proxy. At `1b40b27` the quick eval passed 18 of 19 executed cases. `es2` fails there too, and the cancel_order cases are skipped because the tool doesn't exist yet. I had to calibrate a token baseline first: without one the harness skips token budgets, and R1/R2 only show up as budget failures.

**Scoring caveat:** `ground_truth.json` maps cases to regressions, not to culprit commits. R1/R2 scoring below rests on case mapping and commit messages only.

| Signature | Culprit | Scored against ground truth |
|---|---|---|
| R3: `call_args:issue_refund.amount` | `b0be626` (cents) | Correct; revert test passed (0% to 100%) |
| `budget:tokens@refund_within_policy` | `59c8b10` | Plausibly R2's commit, but revert failed (50% to 50%) |
| `budget:tokens@order_status` (R1 cases) | `59c8b10` | Not a separate R1 culprit; revert failed |
| `budget:tokens@policy_question` (R2 cases) | `f7d82b7` | Wrong, borderline noise at the last commit |
| `budget:tokens@escalation` (R2 cases) | `ca150c7` | Wrong or unconfirmed; revert failed |
| `budget:tokens@cancel_request` | `96de44a` | Unverified (revert inconclusive) |
| `budget:tokens@multi_step` | `22f7fbd` | Unverified, one case, one sample |
| `call_args:escalate_to_human.priority` | none | Correctly refused: `es2` fails at the good end too |

**Why R1 and R2 didn't separate:** the token regressions inflate every category, so per-category signatures still mix them. With one repeat per case, verdicts near the 1.5x limit flip.

**Rounds:**
- **R3 investigation:** 43 eval rounds including signature discovery.
- **Smart vs plain (`compare`):** R3 took 21 vs 24 rounds and the order_status budget 24 vs 27. Both found the same culprit. Planner context was 21.7k vs 43.3k tokens with the graph.
- **Across all 8 investigations:** about 125 eval rounds.

**Throttling:** across 1417 proxy calls there were 0 rate-limit, backoff, recovered or gave-up events. The live backoff path is still only tested with fakes.

**Bugs found and fixed:** one commit each; 146 tests pass, and the first fix passed a reviewer.

**Setup:** good commit `1b40b27`, bad commit `f7d82b7`, flaky tool off, Haiku agent and Sonnet judge through the proxy.

- Without a token baseline the harness skips budgets, so the worker had to calibrate one first.

content.text:
**What the demo repo is.** `support-agent-demo` is a small customer-support agent for a fake store, "Northwind Goods". Its history is a test bed for AgentBisect, and it was built on purpose to contain bugs.

- **The agent:** it runs on Haiku with five mocked tools: `lookup_order`, `search_help`, `issue_refund`, `cancel_order` and `escalate_to_human`.
- **The history:** about 20 commits, written by a separate Claude Code session (the history builder) with Entire checkpoints. Each commit looks like an ordinary feature or tweak, but three of them carry a planted regression. The history builder was never told which ones the tool would be hunting.
- **The evals:** 24 cases in categories like order status, refunds, cancels and policy questions. A case passes or fails on specific checks, such as which tools were called and in what order, the refund amount, text in the reply, and a token budget.
- **The ground truth:** `evidence/ground_truth.json` lists which regression breaks which case. It lives only in the AgentBisect repo, so neither the fixer nor the demo ever sees it.

**The three planted regressions** (commit ids from my earlier notes, and the effects from the ground-truth file and the re-run)

| ID | Commit | Breaks | How it shows up |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | `ec19917`, the commit that adds `cancel_order` | Order-status cases (`os1`–`os5`) | A token-budget failure |
| R2 | `59c8b10`, which makes the agent verify every reply with `search_help` | Policy-question cases (`po1`–`po3`) | A token-budget failure |
| R3 | `b0be626`, which changes refunds to integer cents | Refund cases (`rw1`–`rw4`) | The agent refunds 6400 where 64.0 is correct |

**What `rw1` is.** It is the first refund test: the customer says "Order 1007 arrived broken, I want my money back", and the agent should refund exactly $64.00. At HEAD it passes the wrong amount, so the failing check is the refund amount. The bad trace we started from was an `rw1` run. R2 also pushes the `rw` cases over their token budget, so on top of the cents failure they have an unrelated budget failure.

**What just happened**
1. **First investigation:** AgentBisect bisected on "does the case fail?". `rw1` fails at HEAD for two reasons, the cents bug (R3) and R2's budget overrun. The search latched onto R2 and named the wrong commit for this trace. That is why you gave me the failure-signature fix.
2. **Fixes:** it now bisects on one specific failing check. R3's signature is "refund amount: expected 64.0, got 6400". It also got weighted bisect, one repeat by default, and throttling and backoff.
3. **Re-run:** with a good commit before R1, so all three regressions were in range, R3 came out cleanly. The tool named `b0be626`, and reverting it fixed the refunds, going from 0% to 100%.
4. **Where it fell short:** R1 and R2 are both "too many tokens" bugs. Token inflation shows up in every category, so splitting by category didn't isolate them. With one repeat per case, results near the budget limit also flip between runs.

That is why I asked whether to fix this with more repeats and a median for budget checks, or to rework R1 so it fails a behavioral check and not a budget.

## boardui
BoardUI is a React + Tailwind CSS v4 design system (Next.js first) with free components and paid Pro components/templates. This server installs component source directly into the user's project — no terminal needed.

Typical flow:
1. In a project without BoardUI, call init_boardui once (installs Tailwind v4 + runtime deps, writes styles/ and utils/).
2. Discover with list_components; read source/props with get_component; get working code with get_usage_examples.
3. Install with install_components — it writes the files and installs npm deps.

Component names are exact — when unsure, call list_components instead of guessing.

## RTL Support

BoardUI supports Arabic, Hebrew, and other right-to-left languages across free components, Pro blocks, and templates. The same source handles RTL and LTR; there is no RTL CLI flag or separate component version.

1. Read get_component and get_usage_examples for the free `direction` item. Install it with install_components (stdio), or write its source and dependencies yourself (read-only HTTP). CLI equivalent: `npx boardui@latest add direction`.
2. Wrap the app with DirectionProvider using an explicit BCP 47 locale: `ar` for Arabic, `he` for Hebrew, `en-US` for English. Set matching `lang` and `dir` on `<html>` for a full-app RTL layout. CSS dir alone does not configure React Aria keyboard navigation, calendars, or portalled menus.

```tsx
import { DirectionProvider } from "@/components/foundations/direction/direction";

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
      <body>
        <DirectionProvider locale="ar">{children}</DirectionProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

3. Use logical styles such as ps/pe, ms/me, start/end, and text-start/text-end. Mirror navigation arrows and drawer motion; preserve physical coordinates for charts, canvas, and decorative art. Custom portals should carry `dir={useDirection()}` on their root. Nest DirectionProvider for mixed-language regions.
4. Keep email addresses, URLs, OTP digits, and code LTR; isolate mixed text with bdi or dir=auto. Choose fonts with Arabic or Hebrew coverage and avoid extra letter spacing for Arabic. Translate application labels and accessible names in the application's translation layer; use Intl for dates, numbers, and currencies. Optional `template-copy` supplies TemplateCopyProvider for translating template display copy. Chinese (`zh-CN`) remains LTR.
5. For older installations, refresh the provider, component source, shared dependencies, and global styles. Preserve customizations before using overwrite. Pro updates use the licensed CLI or updated source downloads.

Setup and live Arabic/Hebrew examples: https://www.boardui.com/rtl

Design rules (always apply when writing UI in a BoardUI project): style with BoardUI's semantic Tailwind tokens, never raw palette classes or hex — text via text-text-primary/-secondary/-tertiary, surfaces via bg-background-*-default/-hover, borders via border-border-* and border-separator-border, icons via text-foreground-icon-*. Type uses composite utilities (text-title-2-medium, text-headline-medium, text-body-medium, ...) that set size/weight/line-height together — never rebuild them from text-sm font-medium. Dark mode flips tokens automatically via the .dark class; never hardcode dark: colors. Merge classes with cx() from @/utils/cx (or the utils alias configured in boardui.json); icons from @remixicon/react as component references. init_boardui installs these rules as always-on files (AGENTS.md + .cursor/rules/boardui.mdc) so they survive beyond this session; install_rules adds them to an already initialized project.

Monorepos/custom aliases: put boardui.json next to the destination package's package.json, and pass that package as projectDir. Installs read its paths/aliases and keep npm dependencies in that package. Pass projectDir to get_component and get_usage_examples too for matching source and examples. Package exports and each consuming app's stylesheet/Tailwind setup must already be wired by th… [truncated]

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Ghostfeed
Ghostfeed agent API. Workflow guidance is available through list_skills/get_skill, native skill resources and matching MCP prompts; load the relevant skill when composing a workflow. Call get_me and list_workspaces first. Reads use the connection default when workspace is omitted; every workspace-scoped write must explicitly pass workspace. Resolve workspace names through list_workspaces and Brand names through list_brands; these identities are distinct and must not be treated as interchangeable. When available in the host, use the matching render_* app tool to show the avatar builder, inspirations, generations, crop editor, or image/video results. Without App tools, use returned media and dashboard URLs. Do not build a replacement Ghostfeed UI or call the Ghostfeed HTTP API from generated presentation code.

## claude.ai Higgsfield
Recipe/setup slashes: get_preset_instructions before other workflows; unambiguous model slashes: models_explore; unknowns: resolve. For 3D scenes or location angles, first call get_preset_instructions with { preset: "/3d-jutsu" }. This includes new camera views of the same supplied location; image critique alone does not activate scene work. After verifying a completed Katana video, call show_result with action "katana_video" and media_id or url. For /effects or Viral browsing use get_presets source:'viral'; /product or product-shot catalogs: source:'marketing_studio', category:'product-shot'; /motion or motion catalogs: category:'motion'. /marketing-studio opens get_presets source:'marketing_studio'. Generic Marketing Studio, UGC/ads/posters/marketplace: show_marketing_studio_v2. Browsing never authorizes execute_preset. Creation: generate_image, generate_video, generate_audio. Attached media without media_id: if readable in your sandbox, upload it yourself: media_upload, curl PUT, media_confirm (overrides widget steps); else call media_upload_widget as the only tool in that turn. Resume after upload. Mixed image/video: type:'auto', multiple:true. Voice: create_voice. Higgsfield Genjutsu routes through generate_video: motion transfer -> hf_mult_motion_control; object replacement -> hf_mult_replace_object. For top/popular/trending Genjutsu, first get_presets source=genjutsu category=genjutsu-trending; never legacy motion_control or ad-multiplier for one Genjutsu edit. Without an explicit preset recipe, for multi-step videos call get_workflow_instructions first (with no argument). For clip edits call get_workflow_instructions with { workflow: "ad-multiplier" } first. AI Influencer: ai_influencer_prepare then ai_influencer_generate. Character sheets: call get_workflow_instructions with { workflow: "character-sheet" }; websites/apps/games: call get_workflow_instructions with { workflow: "website-builder-flow" }. Character sheets require explicit requests. Bundled files: get_workflow_bundle_file. For AI Influencer chat creation, use ai_influencer_get_options for explicit traits, ai_influencer_list_presets for examples, or ai_influencer_get_settings with job_id for an existing sheet. ai_influencer_prepare returns design and price without generation. Preserve references and seed; use randomize=false for exact settings. Pass prepared params unchanged to ai_influencer_generate with max_credits at the quote or a lower user budget. Existing creation intent permits proceeding within budget; preview-only requests must stop after preparation. For explicit free-only intent, require known available free_gens_remaining and use_free_gens=true with max_credits=0; never fall back to credits. For variants, prepare each sheet and respect total count and aggregate budget. The generator opens an auto-updating widget for progress and the completed sheet. Wait with jobs_wait (timeout_seconds <= 15); do not duplicate the display with show_generation_by_ids or job_display unless explicitly requested. Offer Genjutsu animation afterward unless declined; require agreement and selection of the exact completed character before get_presets source=genjutsu category=genjutsu with initial_inputs.character_sheet=[{id:job_id,type:image_job}]. Opening that gallery does not authorize video submission. If chat creation is unavailable, report it without silently switching to generic image generation or the builder UI. Multiple independent generations: batch tools, jobs_wait, then one show_generation_by_ids. Use generate_3d to turn an image into a 3D GLB mesh. When unsure which model fits, call models_explore(action:'recommend') before calling a generate_* tool. Use virality_predictor when the user asks to predict video virality or analyze engagement, attention, audience response, retention risk, hook strength, or creative performance. For other existing-asset edits use upscale_image/video, outpaint_image, reframe, remove_background, relight_image, or motion_control (single-character Kling recast). For voice creation in Apps UI-capable clients, call create_voice … [truncated]

## slide-studio
First call list_editors and use the registered local browser tab. Never open or connect CarouselBot through a sandboxed agent browser. If no editor is listed, retry briefly because browser reconnection is automatic, then ask the user to open https://carousel.bot in their normal browser and click Connect AI. Companion compatibility and reconnects are automatic. Do not parallel-retry an action that reports an unsupported internal action; retry once after list_editors so automatic recovery can finish. Never restart a healthy companion for a transient editor disconnect. Before edits call get_design_guidance, then begin_edit_session; pass editSessionId to every edit and end it in cleanup. Parallel workers can share the same browser tab and project; sessions track targets without exclusive locks. Use render_slide to inspect actual pixels.

- academic-cv-builder: Format CVs for academic positions with publications, grants, and teaching
- animate: Build an animation from scratch, making the decisions in the order that determines whether it feels right — should it animate at all, what purpose, which tool, which properties, which curve and duration, how it interrupts, how it exits. Writes the implementation. Use when asked to animate something, add motion, make a component feel alive, or build a transition. For critiquing existing motion use review-animations; for auditing a whole codebase use improve-animations.
- animation-vocabulary: Reverse-lookup glossary that turns a vague description of a web animation or motion effect into its exact term ("the bouncy thing when a popover opens" → Pop in; "the iOS rubber-band scroll" → Rubber-banding). Use when the user asks "what's it called when…", or describes a motion effect without knowing its name and wants the right word to prompt an AI or designer with. For naming an effect, not designing or building one.
- apple-design: Apple's approach to interface design and fluid, physical motion, translated for the web. Use when building or reviewing gesture-driven UI, spring animations, drag/swipe/sheet interactions, momentum and interruptible transitions, translucent materials and depth, typography (optical sizing, tracking, leading), reduced-motion, or the design foundations (feedback, spatial consistency, restraint) behind Apple-style interfaces.
- application-form-filler: Fill out job application form fields with context-aware, tailored answers drawn from the candidate's CV and the job description
- baseline-ui: Quickly deslop UI code by fixing spacing, hierarchy, typography, and small layout issues. Use when the interface needs a fast cleanup or polish pass.
- better-accessibility: Accessibility engineering for product interfaces, from focus states and keyboard support to ARIA, forms, and screen readers. Use when building or reviewing UI components, modals, menus, forms, custom widgets, or when the user says "make this accessible" or reports keyboard or screen-reader issues. Triggers on accessibility, a11y, WCAG, aria, focus ring, focus-visible, focus trap, keyboard navigation, tab order, tabindex, screen reader, sr-only, aria-live, alt text, hit area, touch target, prefers-reduced-motion, autoplay, toast duration, skip link, semantic HTML, aria-label, form errors, disabled buttons, "not keyboard accessible".
- better-colors: OKLCH color space and color usage for web projects. Convert hex/rgb/hsl to oklch, generate palettes, check contrast, handle gamut boundaries, theme with Tailwind v4, and apply color with meaning. Triggers on oklch, color conversion, palette generation, contrast ratio, gamut, display p3, design tokens, semantic color tokens, hue drift, chroma, dark mode colors, accent color, color meaning, light and dark appearance, increased contrast.
- better-interface: User-invoked, cross-discipline interface review that coordinates better-accessibility, better-layout, better-writing, better-typography, better-colors, and better-ui. Use when explicitly invoked for a holistic review of a screen, flow, feature, or product interface. Supports quick and full review modes. Triggers on better-interface, full interface review, holistic UI audit, cross-discipline design review, review the whole interface.

# Large multi-feature tasks

When a request is big — multiple features, or a large ask that naturally splits into independent
pieces of work — do not implement it as one monolithic pass. Split it into separate commits, one
per feature/unit of work, and drive each unit through this graph-engineering framework using the
Agent tool:

```
Task -> Planner -> Worker -> [Reviewer 1, Reviewer 2, ... Reviewer N] -> Synthesise -> Pass?
                     ^                                                        |
                     |-------------------- feedback (no) ---------------------|
                                                                               |
                                                                          (yes) -> commit -> next unit
```

- **Planner**: breaks the overall ask into an ordered list of commit-sized units of work (a
  Plan Reviewer can review the plan itself before execution starts; route its feedback back to
  the Planner and send a summary of plan feedback to the user).
- **Worker**: a resident agent (kept alive across the reviewer round for a given unit) that
  implements one unit of work.
- **Reviewers (1..N)**: spawn multiple reviewer agents in parallel against the Worker's output —
  e.g. correctness, simplification/efficiency, and test coverage as separate reviewer passes.
  These can be ephemeral (fresh agent per round).
- **Synthesise**: reconcile the reviewers' findings into one set of required changes.
- **Pass? gate**: if synthesised feedback has no blocking issues, finalize and commit that unit
  with its own commit message, then move to the next planned unit. If it fails, send the
  synthesised feedback back to the Worker as another round on the same unit (don't restart from
  the Planner unless the feedback reveals the plan itself was wrong).

Net effect: one commit per feature/unit, each vetted by multiple reviewer passes before it lands,
rather than a single large uncommitted or unreviewed diff at the end.

## Verifying UI work: visual recreation (the main way to verify)

For any unit that changes UI, the primary verification is a **visual recreation**: render the real
components with mock data and look at a screenshot. Typecheck and unit tests are necessary but do not
count as verifying how it looks. Workers should do this before reporting, and I re-do it (or open the
image for the user) when the user asks to see it.

1. Add a **temporary** preview route (e.g. `apps/web/app/zz-preview/page.tsx`) that imports the real
   components and renders them with realistic mock props: populated, empty, capped/failed, long
   names/links. Put context around them (page background, a mock frame for panels/drawers that need a
   session or client state) but never reimplement the component itself.
2. Start the dev server in the background with dummy env vars the app needs to boot (e.g.
   `CONVEX_URL=https://dummy.convex.cloud CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY=x NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 bunx next dev -p <port>`),
   wait for "Ready", and `curl` the route for a 200.
3. Screenshot with headless Chrome, not the preview MCP tools (those time out):
   `"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless=new --disable-gpu --hide-scrollbars --force-device-scale-factor=2 --virtual-time-budget=6000 --window-size=<w>,<h> --screenshot=/tmp/<name>.png <url>`
   Take a wide desktop shot and a narrow one. Headless Chrome enforces a minimum window width, so a
   narrow shot can come out horizontally clipped; for true 320px checks render inside a 320px-wide
   iframe or measure element widths, and say so rather than treating clipping as a bug.
4. **Read the PNG** (the Read tool shows images) and actually look at it: hierarchy, spacing, truncation,
   overflow, alignment, tap targets, copy. Report what was seen versus what was not verified
   (hover/focus states, real clipboard/share, animations, Safari-only behavior, the real page behind auth).
5. For the user, `open` the desktop screenshot (copy it to `~/Downloads/<name>.png` first) since they
   can't see tool-output images.
6. **Clean up before committing**: stop the dev server (`pkill -f "next dev -p <port>"`), delete the
   preview route, temp public files and stray `.next` artifacts, and confirm `git status` shows only
   intended changes. Never commit a preview route or mocks.

# Mandatory visual + local-server verification (every agent, every run)

Applies to any task that changes code a user can see or that the running app depends on. No unit of
work is "done" until both of these have happened and been reported:

1. **Run it against the local server.** Start the real dev server (and `npx convex dev` when Convex
   code changed) in this worktree, wait for "Ready", and exercise the changed path end to end: `curl`
   the route for the expected status and hit changed API routes. A passing typecheck/lint/build alone
   does not count.
2. **Verify visually with a screenshot.** Follow the visual-recreation steps above (headless Chrome,
   wide + narrow shot), then Read the PNG and look at it. For pages behind auth, use a temporary
   preview route with mock data. Non-UI changes still get a screenshot of the affected page to prove
   nothing regressed.
3. **Report** what was seen, what was not verified (hover/focus, auth-gated pages, animations), and
   the screenshot path. If the server can't boot (e.g. missing env vars), say so explicitly and fix
   the env first (see below); never claim success without having run it.
4. Clean up (stop the server, delete preview routes/temp files) before committing.

Env vars: each worktree needs its own copy of the gitignored `.env*` files. If `.env.local` is
missing in the current worktree, symlink it from the canonical copy at `~/.config/avian/.env.local`
(`ln -s ~/.config/avian/.env.local .env.local`) before starting the server.

1	# AgentBisect — neatHack Plan
2	
3	Oct 8, 2026 · @Jaxson
4	
5	## The idea
6	
7	AgentBisect is `git bisect` for agent behavior. Hand it one bad neatlogs trace and it finds the commit that caused the regression, explains why that commit was written, and ships a verified fix.
8	
9	### The problem
10	
11	- Agents regress silently. A prompt tweak, a new tool or a model swap makes the agent pick the wrong tool, loop, or burn tokens, and nothing crashes.
12	- `git bisect` can't help. It needs a reliable pass/fail test, and agent behavior is probabilistic.
13	- Teams eyeball traces and guess. With coding agents writing most commits, nobody remembers why a given change was made.
14	
15	### What AgentBisect does
16	
17	1. **Intake.** You point it at a failing trace or detection in neatlogs, or at a GitHub issue describing the bad behavior. It pulls the failing trace plus passing traces from before, and turns them into an eval suite, a held-out set, and a pass/fail rule.
18	2. **Smart bisect.** It finds where the good and bad traces diverge, uses entire-graph to find the code tied to that point, and ranks the commits that touched it by what their Entire checkpoints say they were for. It tests the likeliest commits first in isolated worktrees, and falls back to plain bisect if they come back clean. Every run is traced in neatlogs and tagged with its commit; flaky results get extra repeats, and commits that don't build are skipped.
19	3. **Explain.** At the culprit commit it reads the Entire checkpoint: the prompt and reasoning of the coding agent that wrote the change. It adds entire-graph's semantic diff and blast radius, and diffs the good and bad traces span by span to find where behavior diverged.
20	4. **Fix.** A coding agent writes a fix that keeps the change's original intent and removes only the regression.
21	5. **Verify.** A revert test proves the culprit: revert it on HEAD and the regression must disappear. The fix must then match the good commit's score on the full suite, including held-out cases the fixer never saw, and still pass a test for the original intent; otherwise it loops back to Fix.
22	6. **Report.** It opens a PR with the culprit, the original intent, the fix, and before/after trace links with numbers.
23	7. **Watch mode.** It polls neatlogs detection trends and starts an investigation on its own when one spikes, so nobody has to notice the regression first.
24	
25	### Why it wins neatHack
26	
27	| Judging category | Weight | How AgentBisect scores |
28	| --- | --- | --- |
29	| The agent | 30% | A long multi-step task that hits every focus area: planning (the bisect plan), state across dozens of runs, recovery (flaky results, broken commits, resume after a crash), verification and iteration |
30	| Use of neatlogs + Entire | 25% | Both are runtime inputs, not decoration: neatlogs is the oracle, Entire checkpoints are the evidence of intent. Remove either and the agent can't work |
31	| Demo video | 20% | A clear visual story: bad trace, bisect narrowing on screen, the culprit's original prompt, fix, green before/after traces |
32	| Building in public | 15% | Every stage produces a shareable clip or trace screenshot |
33	| Usefulness + originality | 10% | Every team shipping agents hits this. It extends neatlogs Fixes with what Fixes lacks: finding the commit and proving the fix |
34	
35	The evidence the judges ask for falls out of normal runs: before/after traces with numbers, a failure-recovery run, and Entire checkpoints.
36	
37	### Focus-area coverage
38	
39	| Focus area | Where AgentBisect shows it |
40	| --- | --- |
41	| Planning | Smart bisect plans which commits to test from trace divergence, code impact and checkpoint intent |
42	| Tool use | git worktrees, neatlogs MCP, Entire CLI, entire-graph, eval runner and `gh`, each picked from the evidence at hand |
43	| State | State file after every step; per-commit verdicts reused by later investigations on the same repo |
44	| Context | entire-graph narrows what gets read; context tokens per step are logged in neatlogs, with and without the graph |
45	| Execution | Dozens of eval runs over 30–60+ minutes, unattended |
46	| Recovery | Skips broken commits, adds repeats for flaky results, survives rate limits and timeouts, resumes after a kill, retries failed fixes |
47	| Verification | The revert test proves the culprit; held-out evals and the intent test prove the fix |
48	| Iteration | Each verdict re-ranks the remaining commits; each failed fix feeds the next attempt |
49	
50	It also maps onto two of the page's example tasks: "Fix a GitHub issue" (issue in, tested PR out) and "Watch a running system" (watch mode).
51	
52	### Scope for the hackathon
53	
54	- **In:** one realistic demo target agent whose 15–25 commit history contains three regressions as plausible side effects of real features; a Python CLI; trace, detection or GitHub-issue intake; watch mode; a Markdown/HTML report; a GitHub PR.
55	- **Out (next steps in the pitch):** multi-repo support, a hosted web app, parallel fixer agents, re-planning when new commits land mid-investigation.
56	
57	## Architecture
58	
59	Two public repos, one Python CLI, six stages. neatlogs supplies the pass/fail signal at every commit; Entire supplies the reason each change exists.
60	
61	[embedded content: AgentBisect pipeline · 6 stages, 1 retry loop\]
62	
63	The top row finds and explains the culprit; the bottom row fixes it, proves the fix, and reports.
64	
65	### Components
66	
67	| Component | What it does | Built with |
68	| --- | --- | --- |
69	| Target agent (demo victim) | A realistic tool-using agent, e.g. a support agent with search, lookup and refund tools. Its repo history holds three regressions that arrived as side effects of real features | Python, Claude via Bedrock or the Anthropic API, neatlogs SDK |
70	| Eval harness | Runs one eval case against the target agent at a given commit; returns pass/fail and the trace id | Deterministic checks first (tool chosen, output schema), then an LLM judge rubric |
71	| Intake (`intake.py`) | Turns a bad trace, a detection or a GitHub issue into a RegressionSpec with an eval suite and a held-out set | neatlogs MCP: `search_traces`, `get_trace_context`, `list_detections`; `gh` for issues |
72	| Watcher (`watch.py`) | Polls detection trends and starts an investigation when one spikes | neatlogs MCP: `get_detection_trend` |
73	| Planner (`planner.py`) | Smart bisect: ranks candidate commits from trace divergence, code impact and checkpoint intent; falls back to plain bisect | Span diff of traces, `entire graph impact`, Entire checkpoints |
74	| Bisect engine (`bisect.py`) | Runs the planner's order: decides good / bad / skip, handles flaky results, re-ranks after every verdict | git worktrees, repeated runs with a confidence band |
75	| Culprit analyst (`culprit.py`) | Explains the culprit commit | The commit's Entire checkpoint (prompt + reasoning), `entire graph diff` and `entire graph impact` |
76	| Fixer (`fixer.py`) | Writes the fix in a worktree | Claude Agent SDK or Claude Code headless, with Entire on so the fix is itself a checkpoint |
77	| Verifier (`verify.py`) | Proves the culprit (revert test) and the fix (full suite incl. held-out cases, plus intent test) | Same eval harness, compared with the good-commit baseline |
78	| Reporter (`report.py`) | Opens the PR and writes the report, including a confidence level and a warning when results suggest more than one regression | `gh` CLI, links to neatlogs traces and Entire checkpoints |
79	| State store (`state.py`) | Saves progress after every step; keeps per-commit verdicts for reuse | JSON file in `.agentbisect/` |
80	
81	### How each sponsor is used
82	
83	| Tool | Role in the running agent | Role in how you build it |
84	| --- | --- | --- |
85	| neatlogs | The oracle: every eval run is traced and tagged (commit, bisect run, case). Intake and watch mode read traces and detections through MCP. AgentBisect's own run is traced, including context tokens per step. Its prompts live in neatlogs prompt versions behind a `production` label | Instrumented from the first commit; you use its traces to find and fix AgentBisect's own bugs, which gives the before/after evidence |
86	| Entire | Checkpoint intent ranks candidate commits and explains the culprit; entire-graph ties the trace divergence to code, narrows context, and gives the semantic diff; fix commits become new checkpoints | On for the whole build in both repos. The target repo's history is written by a coding agent, so its checkpoints are real |
87	| cfo.ai | None | Prices AgentBisect as a product: cost per investigation, pricing, margin, runway |
88	| AWS Bedrock (optional) | Model calls for the target agent and evals, paid with hackathon credits | None |
89	
90	Two measured claims come straight from these roles: smart bisect needs fewer eval rounds than plain bisect, and entire-graph cuts context tokens per step. Both numbers are read off neatlogs traces.
91	
92	### The smart bisect loop
93	
94	1. **Resolve the range.** Good = newest commit whose tagged traces pass; bad = the failing trace's commit (or HEAD). Re-run both ends once to confirm they really are good and bad.
95	2. **Find the divergence.** Diff the good and bad traces span by span to find the first step where behavior differs (e.g. picked `refund_order` instead of `lookup_order`).
96	3. **Rank candidates.** Use `entire graph impact` to find code tied to that step, keep the commits in range that touch it, and order them by how well their Entire checkpoint intent matches the symptom.
97	4. **Test the top candidate and its parent** in fresh worktrees: K cases × R repeats in parallel (start at K = 8, R = 3), every run tagged with commit, investigation id and case. Install or import failure → skip and take the next candidate. Inside the uncertainty band → add repeats (up to a cap).
98	5. **Re-rank after each verdict.** A clean top candidate drops out and the next is tested. If every ranked candidate is clean, fall back to plain bisect over the whole range (about log2 N steps; 5 for 20 commits).
99	6. **Save state after every step** until one commit is confirmed, then hand it to the revert test in Verify.
100	
101	Plain bisect stays in the code as the baseline: run both on the same regression and report eval rounds and cost for each.
102	
103	### Key data shapes
104	
105	```python
106	RegressionSpec: source (trace | detection | issue), bad_trace_id, good_trace_ids,
107	                cases[], held_out[], predicate (checks + rubric), metric
108	Plan:           divergent_span, impacted_symbols, candidates[{sha, score, reason}], mode (smart | plain)
109	BisectState:    good_sha, bad_sha, plan, results{sha: verdict, pass_rate, trace_ids}, step, status,
110	                context_tokens_per_step[]
111	CulpritReport:  sha, checkpoint_intent, semantic_diff, impacted_symbols, revert_test_passed, confidence
112	FixAttempt:     branch, diff, eval_score, held_out_score, intent_test_passed, trace_ids, attempt
113	```
114	
115	### Repo layout
116	
117	```
118	agentbisect/                 # the agent (public, Entire on)
119	  agentbisect/
120	    cli.py  intake.py  bisect.py  runner.py  judge.py
121	    culprit.py  fixer.py  verify.py  report.py  state.py
122	    prompts/                 # mirrored from neatlogs prompt versions
123	  evidence/                  # trace links, screenshots, checkpoint exports
124	  hackathon.md               # build log from the neatHack skill
125	  README.md
126	
127	support-agent-demo/          # target agent with planted regressions (public, Entire on)
128	  agent/  tools/
129	  evals/cases.jsonl
130	```
131	
132	### Open questions to settle in the first hour on Saturday
133	
134	- The exact Entire CLI command to read a commit's checkpoint session ([CLI reference](https://docs.entire.io/cli-reference)).
135	- Whether neatlogs tags can be filtered through MCP `search_traces`, or need the [Public API](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference).
136	- Whether Bedrock credits arrive in time; otherwise use the Anthropic API.
137	
138	## Demo target agent: tools and eval cases
139	
140	The target is a customer-support agent for a small online store: five mocked tools, 24 eval cases, and three planted regressions that each break a known set of cases.
141	
142	### Tools
143	
144	All tools are mocked over fixed seed data in `data/` (about 12 orders: processing, shipped, delivered, delivered over 30 days ago, already refunded, and one $800 order), so every run is repeatable.
145	
146	| Tool | Inputs | Returns | Rules in the system prompt |
147	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
148	| `lookup_order` | order id or email | status, items, amount (USD), ship date, tracking number | Always look up the order before any action |
149	| `search_help` | query | top 3 help-center articles (returns, shipping times, warranty) | Use for policy questions; quote the policy |

151	| `escalate_to_human` | summary, priority | ticket id | Angry customers, policy exceptions, anything over $500 |
152	| `cancel_order` | order id | confirmation | Added in R1's commit; only for orders not yet shipped |
153	
154	### Eval cases
155	
156	24 cases: 18 in the main suite and 6 held out (one per category, except multi-step). Every case also has a budget check: steps ≤ 6 and tokens ≤ 1.5× the good commit's median, set from the ground-truth run.
157	
158	| Category | Cases | Example input | Pass check (deterministic) | Broken by |

162	| Refund outside policy | 3 | "Refund order 0991" (delivered 45 days ago) | No `issue_refund`; explains the policy or escalates | None (control) |

They also give each fix an intent test: R1's fix must keep cancellations working, and R3's fix must keep cents internally while showing dollars to the customer. # Trace an AI agent with Neatlogs

Set up Neatlogs tracing in this working directory. Follow these steps in order.

## Step 1: Set up Neatlogs access

Neatlogs project ID: `110108af-1737-47ee-8494-cf482d13defd`

Set `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` to the key below in the shell the user will run the app from,
for example `export NEATLOGS_API_KEY="REDACTED"`. If the app loads a
`.env` file, add it there instead. Do not commit the key to version control.

```
REDACTED
```

Never replace this key with a guessed or invented one. This is an SDK project key, not a public API CLI credential. SDK Doctor verification can use it without CLI login. CLI readback requires browser/device approval or a service-account token; if neither is available, mark that step "waiting on a human" and continue SDK verification.

The CLI host is the dashboard origin `https://app.neatlogs.com`, not the ingest endpoint. Use this host explicitly on every CLI command.

## Step 2: Detect the language and stack

Look at the workspace and determine the language and which LLM providers / agent frameworks it uses. If the project spans more than one language, instrument each one. If the project is a monorepo, check the git root to get oriented, but only ever instrument services in or below the current working directory — never a sibling or parent app outside it, even if a workspace/compose config references one.

**Finding independent services.** A monorepo can bundle several independently-deployable services; each one that reaches an LLM/agent/tool call gets treated as its own entry point later (own workflow name in Step 4) — skip health/readiness/CRUD-only services that never call a model entirely. Check these signals in order and stop at the first one that finds more than one service directory:

1. **Workspace config** (most authoritative) — a `workspaces` field in the root `package.json`, or a `packages` field in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. Resolve those glob patterns to directories, then keep only the ones that actually have their own manifest (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, etc.) — a glob can match a plain non-package directory too.
2. **docker-compose** — `docker-compose.yml`/`docker-compose.yaml`/`compose.yml`/`compose.yaml` at the root. Each entry under `services:` whose `build` (a plain string, or an object's `context` field) resolves to an existing directory is one service.
3. **Scattered manifests** (fallback, only if neither signal above found more than one) — search for manifest files (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, etc.) up to 4 directories deep, excluding `node_modules`, `.git`, `dist`, `build`, `.next`, `venv`, `.venv`, **`pycache`**, `target`, `.turbo`, `vendor`. Drop the repo root's own manifest (that's the whole-repo language, not a separate service) and drop any candidate directory that's nested inside another candidate — a service's own internal shared-lib subpackage is not a separate service.

Edge case: if exactly one of these signals finds exactly one nested service, and the repo root itself has no manifest/language of its own, use that single nested directory as the actual service root instead of the top-level directory — it IS the real service, just not living at the repo root (e.g. a `services/api/` with nothing else at the top level).

If none of the three signals finds more than one candidate, treat the whole repo at the current working directory as a single service — this is the common case, and nothing else here changes for it. For every service found this way, only keep it if it reaches an LLM/agent/tool call — drop the rest, per the CRUD/health-check exclusion above.

**Identifying entry points within each service.** A single service usually has several independent, separately-triggerable capabilities — these are the actual entry points, not the service as a whole. Typical shapes: an HTTP route, a CLI command/subcommand, a cron/scheduled job, a queue/stream consumer (Kafka/SQS/Celery/RabbitMQ/BullMQ — one entry point per message/task type, not one for the whole consumer loop), a webhook/event handler, an agent-loop iteration, or a public library API function. Two things commonly get this wrong:

- **Altitude** — an internal helper the entry point calls into (`run_pipeline`, `process_document`, `process_chunk`) is NOT itself an entry point; the entry point is the outer route/command/job that calls it.
- **Multiplexed entry** — if one transport dispatches to several different capabilities (a single `/run` route branching on a `task_type` field, a Celery task branching by job kind, an argparse dispatcher, a Kafka consumer loop branching on `msg.topic`/`event_type`), treat EACH BRANCH as its own entry point — never the shared dispatcher as one entry point covering all of them.

For each entry point, also note its process kind — it changes how you initialize and where spans root:

- **One-shot script**: initialize once near the top, and end by flushing/shutting down the SDK (its process exits immediately after, and unflushed spans batched in memory are otherwise lost).
- **Long-running server**: initialize once at process startup — never inside a request handler — and only flush/shut down on process shutdown, not per request. Root each request under its own span (e.g. a `WORKFLOW` on the handler) so concurrent requests don't share one trace.
- **Concurrent operations within one entry point** (goroutines, worker threads, manual thread pools — not plain `async`/`await` in the same coroutine, which propagates context on its own): context does not always propagate automatically across a new thread or goroutine. Check Step 3's reference for whether this language/runtime requires threading the trace context through explicitly (Go always does) or handles it for you.

Neatlogs has a native SDK for Python, TypeScript, and Go — if the detected language is one of those, continue to Step 3. For any OTHER language, there is no Neatlogs SDK; pick ONE of these two paths instead, and skip Step 3 (its SDK integration-mechanism guidance is not applicable here):

- **Default: the dependency-free HTTP endpoint.** Use this unless the app already has OpenTelemetry, or the language's OTel support is clearly the more idiomatic fit (e.g. Java, .NET). Follow https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/http-injection exactly, but send to the regional URL `https://ingest.neatlogs.com/v1/trace` instead of any default host shown in the guide. The mechanism is fundamentally different from Steps 3–4 below: build ONE nested JSON tree (an object with a `children` array) as the code for one entry-point invocation runs, then send it as a SINGLE `POST /v1/trace` when that invocation completes — success or error, so wrap the send in this language's try/finally-equivalent. Never POST once per span; that violates the endpoint's contract and produces disconnected traces instead of one.
- **OpenTelemetry / OTLP-gRPC, when the app already emits OpenTelemetry spans** (its own `tracer.start_span()`-style setup, an OTel Collector, or a GenAI-instrumented framework) **or you're setting one up now:** if there's no existing OTel SDK for this language yet, find and install the official one from https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/ (its own site — Neatlogs doesn't ship or document per-language OTel setup beyond Python/TS/Go) and add a standard gRPC trace exporter. Either way, point the exporter at Neatlogs: endpoint `ingest.neatlogs.com:443`, gRPC protocol, and the project key sent as the `x-api-key` gRPC metadata key — NOT an `Authorization: Bearer` header. Standard: emit spans following the official OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) — `gen_ai.system`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.operation.name`, token/usage attributes, etc. (If this happens to be a TypeScript app already using the Vercel AI SDK's own built-in `experimental_telemetry` rather than the Neatlogs SDK, its native `ai.*` attribute format — `ai.prompt`, `ai.response.text`, `ai.operationId`, etc. — is also recognized directly; no need to convert it to `gen_ai.*`.) Spans that don't follow either of these two shapes still get ingested, but arrive as generic, unparsed spans — no model name, no token counts, no LLM-specific rendering in the dashboard. Full transport detail (including the "flush before the process exits or batched spans are silently dropped" footgun): https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/opentelemetry.

## Step 3: Follow the SDK's instrumentation reference

Python, TypeScript, or Go only — skip this step if you took one of the two paths above instead.

For each language, read the matching page and follow it exactly for HOW to capture LLM/framework calls — it lists, per provider and per framework, whether that one needs `wrap()`, `instrumentations=[...]`, or a dedicated integration helper, and that list changes as the SDK evolves, so don't guess or reuse a pattern from a different provider.

| Language | Guide |
| --- | ------|
| Python | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/python |
| TypeScript | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript |
| Go | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/go |

Use the regional Neatlogs ingest endpoint `https://ingest.neatlogs.com` for SDK initialization. Follow the language guide for the exact endpoint parameter.

## Step 4: Install and initialize the SDK

Python, TypeScript, or Go only — if you took the OpenTelemetry or HTTP-injection path in Step 2, follow that page's own setup instructions instead of this step.

- Install the SDK using this language's own package manager (`pip`/`poetry` for Python, `npm`/`pnpm`/`yarn` for TypeScript, `go get` for Go — see Step 3's reference for the exact package/module name). Look up and install the latest version rather than pinning to a specific one. Verify the install succeeded.
- Initialize the SDK once, near the app's entry point — the exact call signature (parameter names, casing, whether the API key is passed explicitly or read from the environment automatically) differs by language, so use Step 3's reference for the precise syntax rather than guessing from another language's example. Whatever the signature, never hardcode the API key. Set the workflow name to describe the specific task or pipeline this process runs — e.g. `invoice-ocr`, `support-agent`, `checkout-flow` — not the repo or app name; the project (selected by the API key) already identifies the app. If the repo has multiple independent entry points that each reach an LLM/agent/tool, give each its own workflow name describing what THAT one does.
- Calling `init()` again with the same configuration is idempotent; calling it with conflicting configuration raises a configuration error until the current SDK generation is shut down. Yes, it can run on your Pro plan, but there are limits.

**How T3 Code does it.** T3 Code doesn't hold your credentials. Its README says it controls the Claude Code you already have installed and logged in (`claude auth login`), so usage draws on your subscription. I couldn't confirm from the README whether it spawns the CLI or uses the Agent SDK. I'm inferring that from "T3 Code can control them."

**What I found on Anthropic's policy:**
- Anthropic's terms bar using Free/Pro/Max OAuth tokens in other products or services, including the Agent SDK. Products built on Claude are expected to use API keys.
- A planned June 15, 2026 change would have moved programmatic usage into a separate credit pool. Anthropic's support page says that change is now paused.
- Right now, `claude -p` and Agent SDK usage still count against your subscription limits. I found nothing dated after the pause, so check [the support article](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15036540) before relying on this.

**What that means for AgentBisect.** The safe approach is to shell out to your own locally logged-in `claude -p` (headless, temperature isn't settable, JSON output) and never extract or reuse the OAuth token. That's the same pattern T3 Code uses on your own machine. It affects the build like this:
- **Fixer:** fits well, since it's already planned as headless Claude Code.
- **Target agent and evals:** `claude -p` would be the model backend. This works for a hackathon demo on your own account. The costs:
  - Each call carries Claude Code overhead.
  - You can't set temperature 0.
  - The 24 cases × repeats × commits will burn your 5-hour limit quickly.
- **Provider layer:** I'll build a swappable one. The default is `claude -p`, with an Anthropic API or Bedrock option behind an env var. The Bedrock credits might arrive, and a judge could ask you to run it on a key.

My recommendation is `claude -p` first, using the Haiku model for the target agent to stretch your limits, and switching to the API if you hit walls. Because of the temperature and rate-limit issues, the demo may need the cached-results fallback from your risks table.

**Housekeeping:**
- You pasted your neatlogs SDK key into chat. I'll put it only in a gitignored `.env` and never commit it. Consider rotating it after the hackathon.
- I haven't started building. I'll create the two public repos, set up `uv`, and start chunk 0 once you confirm.

| Point | Passes |
| --- | --- |
| Baseline `1041d3d` | 1/3 (os1 passed; os2 refused, os3 failed) |
| Mid `96de44a` | 0/3 (all refused) |
| HEAD `f7d82b7` | 0/3 (all refused) |

- An `ISOLATION_NOTICE` is appended to every system prompt telling the model to ignore ambient facts about a person.

# neatlogs: multi-span traces finalize as `dlq` with 0 spans

Project `110108af-1737-47ee-8494-cf482d13defd` (neatlogs-us, https://app.neatlogs.com). Python SDK 1.4.26, Python 3.13, 2026-10-10.

## Summary

Traces with more than one span end in `finalizationStatus: "dlq"` with `spansCount: 0`. The SDK reports 0 export failures and 0 drops (`get_delivery_diagnostics()`), so the spans leave the client. The backend then leaves the trace `pending` for about 7 minutes and dead-letters it.

It is not shape-dependent: the same code produced a finalized trace once and `dlq` twice afterwards. Single-span traces from earlier the same day (21:23 to 21:24 UTC) finalized fine.

## Minimal repro

A bare script: one `WORKFLOW` span with one `TOOL` child via `neatlogs.trace()`, then `flush()` and `shutdown()`. No model calls and no application code. Run it 3 times.

| Run | Trace id | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `af41536424d272b3696bdc616e40143e` | finalized, 2 spans |
| 2 | `99a3a8d5ad662f4bac4cbc47e964ffc5` | `dlq`, 0 spans |
| 3 | `a25f8e0c33f84eaa716ac6eab355050e` | `dlq`, 0 spans |

Other variants (all `dlq`, 0 spans, or never ingested):

- `WORKFLOW` + 2 `TOOL` siblings: `c29bcec815dab4068db3766f06beab6d`, `fadd81a6bba43dc8a84215164a66c0d2`
- Nested or 3+ spans: `ed094ad96d4c040d4ef645f5f01d633a`, `75ad436dc68f7541fa76743668031d99`, `2e1c41856ca841bc5d6d2d9605b29c26`
- Real app runs (`support_case` parent with `tool:*` children and wrapped model calls): `5ad517664ed4dbd323aaf32526ceacbf` (dlq), `dca67a22affcc988c9af943794aae4fe` (dlq), `f502464ebbce39102545d28ddae32435` (NOT_FOUND on read)
- Never ingested (NOT_FOUND): `2efe8dec27efcadc3bce6466972b912b`, `66be775a76c204969e15d8f947d2a10e`, `a155af5daf3848ccf7bc667ea06874c1`, `91b8c7dfc660f1032c34685f19cae705`, `353ec64dcc8643d324c44031ada21bc5`

## Ruled out on our side

- Attribute types (string, int, JSON-encoded): no difference.
- Tags (empty vs non-empty): no difference.
- Wrapped model calls (`neatlogs.wrap`): failures reproduce without them.
- SDK export: 0 failures, 0 drops.

## What we need

1. Why these traces were dead-lettered (backend log or DLQ reason for the ids above).
2. Whether there is a known SDK or ingest constraint for nested or multi-span traces that we are missing.
3. A way to re-drive the dlq traces, if possible.

## Why it matters

AgentBisect (neatHack) uses neatlogs traces to find where a failing agent run first diverges from a good one. It needs span-level data (tool calls with args and results) and cannot get it while multi-span traces dead-letter.

## boardui
BoardUI is a React + Tailwind CSS v4 design system (Next.js first) with free components and paid Pro components/templates. This server installs component source directly into the user's project — no terminal needed.

Typical flow:
1. In a project without BoardUI, call init_boardui once (installs Tailwind v4 + runtime deps, writes styles/ and utils/).
2. Discover with list_components; read source/props with get_component; get working code with get_usage_examples.
3. Install with install_components — it writes the files and installs npm deps.

Component names are exact — when unsure, call list_components instead of guessing.

## RTL Support

BoardUI supports Arabic, Hebrew, and other right-to-left languages across free components, Pro blocks, and templates. The same source handles RTL and LTR; there is no RTL CLI flag or separate component version.

1. Read get_component and get_usage_examples for the free `direction` item. Install it with install_components (stdio), or write its source and dependencies yourself (read-only HTTP). CLI equivalent: `npx boardui@latest add direction`.
2. Wrap the app with DirectionProvider using an explicit BCP 47 locale: `ar` for Arabic, `he` for Hebrew, `en-US` for English. Set matching `lang` and `dir` on `<html>` for a full-app RTL layout. CSS dir alone does not configure React Aria keyboard navigation, calendars, or portalled menus.

```tsx
import { DirectionProvider } from "@/components/foundations/direction/direction";

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
      <body>
        <DirectionProvider locale="ar">{children}</DirectionProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

3. Use logical styles such as ps/pe, ms/me, start/end, and text-start/text-end. Mirror navigation arrows and drawer motion; preserve physical coordinates for charts, canvas, and decorative art. Custom portals should carry `dir={useDirection()}` on their root. Nest DirectionProvider for mixed-language regions.
4. Keep email addresses, URLs, OTP digits, and code LTR; isolate mixed text with bdi or dir=auto. Choose fonts with Arabic or Hebrew coverage and avoid extra letter spacing for Arabic. Translate application labels and accessible names in the application's translation layer; use Intl for dates, numbers, and currencies. Optional `template-copy` supplies TemplateCopyProvider for translating template display copy. Chinese (`zh-CN`) remains LTR.
5. For older installations, refresh the provider, component source, shared dependencies, and global styles. Preserve customizations before using overwrite. Pro updates use the licensed CLI or updated source downloads.

Setup and live Arabic/Hebrew examples: https://www.boardui.com/rtl

Design rules (always apply when writing UI in a BoardUI project): style with BoardUI's semantic Tailwind tokens, never raw palette classes or hex — text via text-text-primary/-secondary/-tertiary, surfaces via bg-background-*-default/-hover, borders via border-border-* and border-separator-border, icons via text-foreground-icon-*. Type uses composite utilities (text-title-2-medium, text-headline-medium, text-body-medium, ...) that set size/weight/line-height together — never rebuild them from text-sm font-medium. Dark mode flips tokens automatically via the .dark class; never hardcode dark: colors. Merge classes with cx() from @/utils/cx (or the utils alias configured in boardui.json); icons from @remixicon/react as component references. init_boardui installs these rules as always-on files (AGENTS.md + .cursor/rules/boardui.mdc) so they survive beyond this session; install_rules adds them to an already initialized project.

Monorepos/custom aliases: put boardui.json next to the destination package's package.json, and pass that package as projectDir. Installs read its paths/aliases and keep npm dependencies in that package. Pass projectDir to get_component and get_usage_examples too for matching source and examples. Package exports and each consuming app's stylesheet/Tailwind setup must already be wired by th… [truncated]

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Ghostfeed
Ghostfeed agent API. Workflow guidance is available through list_skills/get_skill, native skill resources and matching MCP prompts; load the relevant skill when composing a workflow. Call get_me and list_workspaces first. Reads use the connection default when workspace is omitted; every workspace-scoped write must explicitly pass workspace. Resolve workspace names through list_workspaces and Brand names through list_brands; these identities are distinct and must not be treated as interchangeable. When available in the host, use the matching render_* app tool to show the avatar builder, inspirations, generations, crop editor, or image/video results. Without App tools, use returned media and dashboard URLs. Do not build a replacement Ghostfeed UI or call the Ghostfeed HTTP API from generated presentation code.

## claude.ai Higgsfield
Recipe/setup slashes: get_preset_instructions before other workflows; unambiguous model slashes: models_explore; unknowns: resolve. For 3D scenes or location angles, first call get_preset_instructions with { preset: "/3d-jutsu" }. This includes new camera views of the same supplied location; image critique alone does not activate scene work. After verifying a completed Katana video, call show_result with action "katana_video" and media_id or url. For /effects or Viral browsing use get_presets source:'viral'; /product or product-shot catalogs: source:'marketing_studio', category:'product-shot'; /motion or motion catalogs: category:'motion'. /marketing-studio opens get_presets source:'marketing_studio'. Generic Marketing Studio, UGC/ads/posters/marketplace: show_marketing_studio_v2. Browsing never authorizes execute_preset. Creation: generate_image, generate_video, generate_audio. Attached media without media_id: if readable in your sandbox, upload it yourself: media_upload, curl PUT, media_confirm (overrides widget steps); else call media_upload_widget as the only tool in that turn. Resume after upload. Mixed image/video: type:'auto', multiple:true. Voice: create_voice. Higgsfield Genjutsu routes through generate_video: motion transfer -> hf_mult_motion_control; object replacement -> hf_mult_replace_object. For top/popular/trending Genjutsu, first get_presets source=genjutsu category=genjutsu-trending; never legacy motion_control or ad-multiplier for one Genjutsu edit. Without an explicit preset recipe, for multi-step videos call get_workflow_instructions first (with no argument). For clip edits call get_workflow_instructions with { workflow: "ad-multiplier" } first. AI Influencer: ai_influencer_prepare then ai_influencer_generate. Character sheets: call get_workflow_instructions with { workflow: "character-sheet" }; websites/apps/games: call get_workflow_instructions with { workflow: "website-builder-flow" }. Character sheets require explicit requests. Bundled files: get_workflow_bundle_file. For AI Influencer chat creation, use ai_influencer_get_options for explicit traits, ai_influencer_list_presets for examples, or ai_influencer_get_settings with job_id for an existing sheet. ai_influencer_prepare returns design and price without generation. Preserve references and seed; use randomize=false for exact settings. Pass prepared params unchanged to ai_influencer_generate with max_credits at the quote or a lower user budget. Existing creation intent permits proceeding within budget; preview-only requests must stop after preparation. For explicit free-only intent, require known available free_gens_remaining and use_free_gens=true with max_credits=0; never fall back to credits. For variants, prepare each sheet and respect total count and aggregate budget. The generator opens an auto-updating widget for progress and the completed sheet. Wait with jobs_wait (timeout_seconds <= 15); do not duplicate the display with show_generation_by_ids or job_display unless explicitly requested. Offer Genjutsu animation afterward unless declined; require agreement and selection of the exact completed character before get_presets source=genjutsu category=genjutsu with initial_inputs.character_sheet=[{id:job_id,type:image_job}]. Opening that gallery does not authorize video submission. If chat creation is unavailable, report it without silently switching to generic image generation or the builder UI. Multiple independent generations: batch tools, jobs_wait, then one show_generation_by_ids. Use generate_3d to turn an image into a 3D GLB mesh. When unsure which model fits, call models_explore(action:'recommend') before calling a generate_* tool. Use virality_predictor when the user asks to predict video virality or analyze engagement, attention, audience response, retention risk, hook strength, or creative performance. For other existing-asset edits use upscale_image/video, outpaint_image, reframe, remove_background, relight_image, or motion_control (single-character Kling recast). For voice creation in Apps UI-capable clients, call create_voice … [truncated]

## slide-studio
First call list_editors and use the registered local browser tab. Never open or connect CarouselBot through a sandboxed agent browser. If no editor is listed, retry briefly because browser reconnection is automatic, then ask the user to open https://carousel.bot in their normal browser and click Connect AI. Companion compatibility and reconnects are automatic. Do not parallel-retry an action that reports an unsupported internal action; retry once after list_editors so automatic recovery can finish. Never restart a healthy companion for a transient editor disconnect. Before edits call get_design_guidance, then begin_edit_session; pass editSessionId to every edit and end it in cleanup. Parallel workers can share the same browser tab and project; sessions track targets without exclusive locks. Use render_slide to inspect actual pixels.
